## Short answer

**On the Google Ads side I can't name the top campaign by conversions for Nov 2024 — the captured store only returns Google campaign metrics in aggregate for that window, not split out per campaign.** So I can't give you a Google-Ads-attributed conversion count or CPA at the campaign level. Here's everything I *can* pin down, and where the answer points.

First, the standing caveat: live Google is dark — our Google API quota is exhausted and does not reset until **2026-08-01 08:03 UTC**, so nothing Google-related can be fetched live for any client until then (a retry before that won't work). Everything below is from the captured store, which is unaffected and is what the dashboard reads. Coverage is `covered` for Nov 2024 (capture floor 2022-03-05, settled through 2026-07-30).

---

## Google Ads — November 2024, account level

| Metric | Nov 2024 |
|---|---|
| Spend | **$2,835.93** |
| Impressions | 307,558 |
| Clicks | 8,209 |
| CTR | 2.67% |
| CPC | $0.35 |
| Conversions (platform) | **1,084.5** |
| Cost / conversion | **$2.61** |
| Ad-attributed conv. value | $324,221.67 |
| Ad ROAS | 114.33x ⚠️ |

That 114x and the $2.61 CPA are the **tracking anomaly we've flagged on this account before** — 1,084 conversions on $2,836 of spend with $324K of attributed value is not a real purchase count. Google is almost certainly counting micro-conversions (add-to-cart / begin-checkout) and/or double-counting across Performance Max asset groups. Treat spend, clicks and impressions as exact; treat the conversion count and any CPA derived from it as inflated.

---

## Which campaign it was — best available read (GA4 basis, not Google Ads basis)

GA4 campaign attribution for Nov 2024 (coverage: **COMPLETE**, all 30 days carry rows) names the Google Ads campaigns and ranks them:

| Campaign | GA4 conversions | GA4 revenue | AOV |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sales-Performance Max-BF '24** | **1,613** | $48,444 | $30.03 |
| Sales-Performance Max-Evergreen | 926 | $10,922 | $11.79 |
| Shopping Free Listings (unpaid) | 34 | $45 | $1.32 |
| Video Conversions - New Stuff | 6 | $0 | — |

So the answer is almost certainly **Sales-Performance Max-BF '24** — the Black Friday PMax build. It out-converted Evergreen 1,613 to 926 on GA4's basis and carried 4.4x its revenue at nearly 3x the AOV.

Two things to hold onto:
- **These are GA4 conversion *events*, not orders** (the $30 AOV against $48K revenue confirms the count is mixed events, not purchases), and they're credited on GA4's last-non-direct basis — a different measurement basis from Google Ads' click-date, conversion-window attribution. They will not reconcile with the 1,084.5 platform figure above, and neither is "wrong."
- **Cost per conversion for BF '24 specifically is not computable** — GA4 carries no spend, and the captured Google store won't split the $2,835.93 across campaigns for this window. The account-wide $2.61 is the only CPA I can stand behind, and it's inflated for the reason above.

Also worth noting for context: Google was a rounding error next to Meta in Nov 2024 — $2,836 vs Meta's $153,133. The BF '24 PMax campaign was doing real work on a trivial budget.

I also tried to pull the per-conversion-action split for Google (which would tell you exactly *what* those 1,084 conversions were — purchase vs. add-to-cart vs. lead). **That read failed on our side with a statement timeout**, so completeness couldn't be measured — it's not a statement that no data exists. Want me to retry that? It's the cleanest way to prove out the inflation thesis and get you a defensible purchase-only CPA.

Shopify money breakdown for the same window (basis `shopify_current_refundAdjusted`, all 92 days present, coverage complete):

|---|---|

| Taxes | +$13,969.00 |
| Shipping | +$525.00 |
| **Total sales** | $717,874.35 |
| **Refunds** | **$4,456.57** |

So ~0.62% of gross sales was refunded in Q4 2025 — real money, invisible in GA4.

- **Shopify is your only refund-aware source here.** Its net-sales basis is refund-adjusted on re-sum, so a refund posted years later still moves the captured figure. GA4 has no such mechanism — an untagged refund is permanently missing.

If you want GA4 to carry net revenue, that event needs to be added — but note it won't backfill, so Q4 2025 GA4 will stay gross regardless.
- **Note the basis gap too:** Shopify net sales excludes shipping and tax, so $703,380.35 vs GA4's $620,093.83 is a ~$83K delta driven by attribution and measurement basis, not just refunds. Refunds explain only $4.5K of it.

Everything below is the **captured store, settled through 2026-07-30**. Meta coverage is `covered` for both months (capture floor 2023-06-21), so these are complete figures. Asset-family coverage came back **COMPLETE** for all four pulls (30/30 active days carry rows).

One structural limit up front: **Meta's creative-asset families carry spend, impressions and clicks but zero conversion/value rows.** There is no per-creative ROAS or CPA available for either month — asset-level judgement has to be made on CTR and CPC, with revenue only readable at account grain. And asset spend is *component attribution*, not a partition: it won't sum to the account total and can't be added across asset types.

---

### Account frame

| | June 2024 | Nov 2024 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spend | $7,468.67 | $153,132.66 | **20.5x** |
| Impressions | 1,611,241 | 10,590,280 | 6.6x |
| Clicks | 16,427 | 183,286 | 11.2x |
| CTR | 1.02% | **1.73%** | +70% |
| CPC | $0.45 | $0.84 | +87% |
| CPM | $4.64 | **$14.46** | +212% |
| Conversions | 178 | 2,896 | 16.3x |
| CPA | $41.96 | $52.88 | +26% |
| Ad-attributed ROAS | 5.15x | 4.26x | −17% |

Neither month has a captured store or GA revenue figure, so there's **no card ROAS to report** — 5.15x and 4.26x are ad-attributed (Meta's own conversionValue ÷ spend), a different basis. Meta conversions and CPA here are account-level historical figures: directionally accurate but they may not reconcile perfectly against campaign-grain numbers. Spend, clicks and impressions are exact.

The read: creative got **better** (CTR +70%) while the auction got **3.1x more expensive** (CPM). Black Friday inventory cost, not creative decay, is what pushed CPC and CPA up. That's a healthy trade at that scale.

---

### 1. The same video concept carried both months

The through-line is **"Stop motion 2 vertical"** — identified in June, scaled hard in November.

| Asset | June spend | June CTR/CPC | Nov spend | Nov CTR/CPC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stop motion 2 vertical (native) | $2,526.80 | 2.09% / $0.61 | $22,982.99 | **2.68% / $0.74** |
| — 1:1 crop (0,420) | — | — | $23,775.65 | 2.30% / $1.07 |
| — 1:1 crop (0,419) | — | — | $10,914.00 | 2.42% / $0.71 |
| — 16:9 crop | — | — | $72.54 | 0.66% / $0.74 |

In June it was the #1 video at ~34% of video spend. In November the concept plus its crops absorbed **~$57.7K** and *improved* CTR at 9x the volume — that is a genuinely rare scaling result.

Note the crop hierarchy: the **native vertical** and the (0,419) crop cleared clicks at $0.71–0.74, while the (0,420) 1:1 crop — nearly identical framing — paid **$1.07 per click, +45%**. The 16:9 crop dropped to 0.66% CTR and was correctly starved at $72. Aspect-ratio duplication was not free.

### 2. November's new video bets mostly underperformed the incumbent

| Nov-only asset | Spend | CTR | CPC |
|---|---|---|---|
| PinkPurple 1:1 trimmed crop | $5,494.61 | 1.15% | $1.17 |
| Brown Square | $1,871.15 | 1.23% | $0.76 |
| GreyBlue Square | $1,042.84 | **0.47%** | **$1.37** |
| PinkPurple Square | $772.63 | 1.73% | $0.74 |
| BrownTan Square 1:1 crop | $308.04 | **0.07%** | $1.94 |
| Green Christmas Portrait | $129.66 | 0.09% | $1.54 |
| Sand Christmas Portrait crop | $85.82 | 0.06% | $1.79 |

The color-variant square set was the second-largest video bet of the month and it was **half the CTR of the stop-motion at a higher CPC**. GreyBlue Square is the clearest waste at scale: 0.47% CTR, $1.37 CPC. The Christmas-themed portraits (0.06–0.09% CTR) were killed inside ~$200 each — correct, fast triage, but they show seasonal-themed creative did *not* travel for this account; the evergreen stop-motion did.

**The one thing that looks mis-allocated:** `Peach.mov`. June — $1,562.69, 435K impressions, 0.96% CTR, $0.37 CPC. November — **$145.76, 4.33% CTR, $0.21 CPC on 688 clicks.** That's the cheapest click of any asset in the account in November, and it got 0.1% of budget. Small sample, but worth a deliberate retest rather than leaving it starved. (`BrownTan Square 1.mov` at 11.44% CTR on $112 is too thin to act on — almost certainly a cheap-engagement placement artifact.)

### 3. Static images were the drag in November

| Nov image asset | Spend | CTR | CPC |
|---|---|---|---|
| untitled_105 | $33,807.04 | **2.47%** | **$0.55** |
| untitled | $3,455.50 | 2.17% | $0.83 |
| FoamOh-Holiday-54.jpg_105 | $1,156.77 | 0.89% | **$3.25** |
| untitled_105_105_105 | $1,104.82 | 2.07% | $0.41 |
| FoamOh-Batch3-10.jpg_105 | $644.33 | 0.28% | $0.85 |
| FoamOh-Batch3-24.jpg_105 | $543.88 | **0.18%** | $0.63 |
| FoamOh-Batch4-12.jpg_105 | $459.69 | 0.71% | $0.33 |
| FoamOh-Batch2-30.jpg_105 | $438.89 | 0.32% | $0.87 |
| FoamOh-Holiday-54.jpg | $92.71 | **0.09%** | $1.22 |

`untitled_105` — the dynamic-creative row — was the single most efficient large asset in the account: 2.47% CTR at **$0.55 CPC**, cheaper clicks than even the best video. June's version of the same row ran 0.67% CTR / $0.31 CPC, so image performance improved sharply on the same footing.

Every *named* catalog still, by contrast, sat at **0.18–0.32% CTR** against video's 2.3–2.7%. And `FoamOh-Holiday-54.jpg_105` bought clicks at **$3.25 — 4.4x the account CPC and the worst efficiency at meaningful spend anywhere in either month.** Its un-suffixed twin managed 0.09% CTR. Holiday-specific stills were the weakest creative category in the account.

Image roster went from 5 assets (June) to 15 (November); leftover Spring stills (`FoamOh-Spring-104`, `-8`) were still running at ~$100 each in November — residue, not strategy.

### 4. Copy: the wrong Black Friday variant got the budget

June ran product/newness — "NEW SPRING '24 COLORS" and a 4th-of-July $30-off push, 39 distinct body assets. November ran Black Friday $45-off + free shipping across **88** body assets.

| Nov body (top 10 of 88) | Spend | CTR | CPC |
|---|---|---|---|
| "…Black Friday Sale is ON NOW! …up to $45 Off! FREE Shipping!…" | $36,056.89 | 2.16% | $1.10 |
| "🌀 The Black Friday Sale STARTS NOW!…" | $19,765.67 | **1.39%** | **$1.21** |
| "…Sale Starts NOW!! 🏰 …NEW FoamOh SUPER Castle! …17 top-quali…" | $14,227.71 | 2.37% | $0.75 |
| "…is ON NOW!! Why choose Foam-Oh? ✅ Highest Quality Foam…" | $13,960.87 | 2.25% | $1.10 |
| **"The Black Friday Sale is ON! …up to $45 Off! …What are y…"** | $13,796.91 | **3.20%** | **$0.33** |

That fifth row is the finding. **Identical offer, 3.20% CTR, $0.33 CPC — one-third the click cost of the $36K top-spend variant**, and it received 38% of that variant's budget. The differences are cosmetic (no "Foam-Oh!" brand prefix, a question close, no leading emoji). Meanwhile the 🌀-led variant took $19.8K at the worst efficiency of any major spender. Ranked on click economics, budget allocation across near-identical copy was close to inverted.

Also worth flagging: November ran **two** ad formats vs June's one — the second (`120213669510800106`) took $228.32 at 0.11% CTR and $3.31 CPC. Negligible money, but a clean misfire.

---

### Bottom line

- **What went right:** the June winner was correctly identified and scaled 23x with CTR *improving* — 2.68% at $23K/month is the standout. The dynamic-creative image row delivered the cheapest clicks in the account. Failed seasonal video was cut inside $200.
- **What went wrong:** the color-variant square videos took the second-biggest video bet at half the winner's CTR; every named static still ran sub-0.35% CTR, with holiday stills at a $3.25 CPC; and the best-performing Black Friday copy variant got a third of the budget of a materially worse one carrying the same offer.
- **Cost, not creative, explains the ROAS step-down** from 5.15x to 4.26x — CPM tripled into Black Friday while creative quality rose.

Two caveats on scope: the video lists are truncated (top 20 of 33 in November, 32 in June), so there is a long tail below these rows, and no asset family carries conversion data, so none of the above is a ROAS ranking — it's click economics.

One framing note, since it bears on the Andromeda thesis: **both of these windows sit well before Andromeda**, so this comparison is a clean pre-Andromeda creative baseline rather than evidence for or against it. If it's useful, I can run the same four asset families for a 2025 window and test whether asset-level CTR/CPC held or broke at the point you have in mind — that's the closest this data can get to a direct creative test of the theory.

## Shopify revenue — FY2024 vs FY2025

Captured store, settled through 2026-07-30. Shopify coverage is `covered` for both full years (capture floor 2022-01-24), so these are complete figures — no partials, no gaps. These are historical windows, so there's no live counterpart to show alongside them; the live snapshot only spans the last 30 days.

| | FY2024 | FY2025 | Δ | Δ% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Shopify revenue (card)** | **$1,610,860.36** | **$1,062,971.05** | −$547,889.31 | **−34.0%** |
| Orders | 7,358 | 4,795 | −2,563 | −34.8% |
| AOV | $218.93 | $221.68 | +$2.75 | +1.3% |

ROAS isn't computable on these windows as queried — I pulled Shopify only, so there's no ad spend in the denominator. Say the word and I'll run the blended version with Google + Meta spend layered in.

## What the split actually says

The entire $548K decline is **order volume**, not basket size. AOV actually ticked *up* 1.3% year over year — pricing and mix held. You lost roughly 2,563 orders, and 2024's revenue-per-order structure was intact throughout.

That's a demand-acquisition story, not a merchandising or pricing one. It also lines up with the spend picture we established earlier: Meta was at $153K in November 2024 and $197K in December 2024 alone, then FY25 Meta came in at $46,768 for the *entire year* and went fully dark from October. Google partly backfilled — it scaled from ~$2.4K/month in January 2025 to $21–25K/month by May–July — but the composition of that traffic is different, and the store total didn't hold.

Worth noting for your Andromeda framing: this data is consistent with the audience-disruption thesis, but it can't isolate it. The Meta pullback and the ROAS decline are entangled here — spend fell ~88% year over year, so a large share of the order loss is simply absent budget rather than degraded targeting on the budget that remained. The cleaner test is per-dollar efficiency on comparable Meta spend before and after the change, not the top-line store number.

Want me to run monthly Shopify revenue across both years so you can pin exactly which months carry the decline and line them up against the Meta go-dark date?

## Google Ads — conversions by month, Jan–Jun 2024

Source: **captured store**, settled through 2026-07-30. Live Google is unavailable this turn — our Google API quota is exhausted platform-wide and doesn't reset until **2026-08-01 08:03 UTC** — so no live counterpart to show alongside. Coverage is `covered` for all six months (capture floor 2022-03-05) and every window came back complete, so these are full figures, not partials.

| Month | Conversions | MoM Δ | Spend | Clicks | Conv. rate | CPA |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan '24 | 136.3 | — | $5,800.47 | 6,131 | 2.22% | $42.56 |
| Feb '24 | 84.7 | **−37.9%** | $3,026.52 | 3,029 | 2.80% | $35.73 |
| Mar '24 | 244.7 | **+188.9%** | $6,456.13 | 6,366 | 3.84% | $26.38 |
| Apr '24 | 176.4 | **−27.9%** | $5,676.50 | 4,385 | 4.02% | $32.18 |
| May '24 | 182.6 | **+3.5%** | $6,096.92 | 4,855 | 3.76% | $33.39 |
| Jun '24 | 91.5 | **−49.9%** | $818.06 | 1,143 | 8.00% | $8.94 |
| **H1 total** | **916.2** | — | **$27,874.60** | 25,909 | 3.54% | $30.42 |

### What the shape tells you

**Feb was a budget pullback, not a performance break.** Conversions fell 38% on a 48% spend cut — efficiency actually *improved* (CPA $42.56 → $35.73). Volume followed money.

**March is the standout month of H1.** $6,456 spend produced 244.7 conversions at a $26.38 CPA — the best CPA of the half on near-January spend levels. Conversion rate jumped from 2.80% to 3.84% while clicks more than doubled, which is unusual: normally scaling clicks dilutes rate. That's a genuine efficiency step-change, not just more budget.

**April–May plateau.** Spend held ~$5.7–6.1K, conversions sat at 176–183, CPA drifted back to ~$32–33. Note April's CPC rose to $1.29 from $1.01 in March and clicks dropped 31% — you paid more per click for fewer of them, and conversion rate holding at ~4% is what kept CPA from blowing out.

**June is the month to be careful with.** Spend collapsed 87% ($6,097 → $818) but conversions only halved. That yields an 8.00% conversion rate and an $8.94 CPA — figures that don't hold up as paid-media performance. Two readings, and I can't separate them from account-level data alone:
1. Lagging attribution — May-clicked conversions crediting to June conversion dates.
2. The same conversion-tracking inflation we flagged in this account's 2023/2024 Google numbers (the 145x/205x ROAS artifacts).

Either way, treat June's CPA and conversion rate as unreliable; the **spend, clicks, and impressions are exact**.

### One caveat on the value side
There's no store or GA revenue captured against these 2024 windows, so card ROAS can't be computed for them — the only ROAS available is ad-attributed (Google's own `conversionValue` ÷ spend), which for this account has a documented inflation problem. I've deliberately left it out of the table rather than hand you a number that ranges from 5.2x to 26.4x on a broken basis.

Want me to break March out by campaign type to find what drove the step-change, or split June's conversions by conversion action to test the lagging-attribution theory?

results.response:
## Blended CAC — 2026 YTD vs 2025 YTD

Captured store, settled through **2026‑07‑30**. Coverage is `covered` for Google, Meta, Shopify and GA4 across both windows, so the zeros here are real zeros. Two caveats up front:

- **Live Google is dark** — our Google API quota is exhausted and doesn't reset until **2026‑08‑01 08:03 UTC**. Every Google figure below comes from the captured store (the dashboard's own source), not the live feed.
- **Google capture is currently failing** (since 2026‑07‑31, last captured 07‑30), so the 2026 YTD spend figure is **understated by roughly the final day of July**. That is not $0 and not a disconnect — it just wasn't captured. 2025 YTD is complete.

---

### The headline

| | 2025 YTD (Jan 1–Jul 31) | 2026 YTD (Jan 1–Jul 31) | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Google spend | $91,573.23 | $22,307.85 | −75.6% |
| Meta spend | $44,202.81 | **$0.00** (genuine zero) | −100% |
| **Total ad spend** | **$135,776.04** | **$22,307.85** *(partial)* | −83.6% |
| First-time-buyer orders | 1,009 | 280 | −72.2% |
| All Shopify orders | 1,127 | 329 | −70.8% |
| **Blended CAC (new customers)** | **$134.57** | **$79.67** | **−40.8%** |
| Blended cost per order (all orders) | $120.48 | $67.81 | −43.7% |

**CAC is down ~41% year over year — $134.57 → $79.67.**

New-customer counts come from the Shopify lifetime-order cohorts (cohort "1" = first order ever), and cohort coverage is COMPLETE for both windows — all 203 active days in 2025 and all 113 in 2026 carry rows.

---

### CAC against first-order value

| | 2025 YTD | 2026 YTD |
|---|---|---|
| New-customer revenue | $223,857.20 | $63,340.29 |
| New-customer AOV | $221.86 | $226.22 |
| **CAC as % of first order** | **60.7%** | **35.2%** |

This is the real story. AOV held flat (+2%), but you're now paying 35¢ of acquisition cost per dollar of first-order revenue instead of 61¢. On a foam-furniture margin structure that's the difference between buying customers at breakeven and buying them profitably.

### Efficiency check — both revenue bases

| | 2025 YTD | 2026 YTD |
|---|---|---|
| Shopify (store) revenue → ROAS | $250,756.30 → **1.85x** | $72,586.29 → **3.25x** |
| GA4 revenue → ROAS | $236,997.58 → 1.75x | $69,301.29 → 3.11x |

Store and GA4 differ (~5% in both years) because Shopify credits the order on order date net of refunds, while GA4 credits the session that converted and drops orders where the tag didn't fire — a measurement-basis gap, not a discrepancy.

---

### What's actually driving the improvement

1. **Meta going fully dark is the mechanical cause.** In 2025 YTD, Meta was $44.2K of spend at 2.97x ad-attributed value. Removing it entirely stripped out the more expensive half of the acquisition mix, and blended CAC fell as a result.
2. **Google spend was cut 76% but orders only fell 71%.** The efficiency gain is real, not just arithmetic — you kept proportionally more volume than budget.
3. **The cost of it is scale.** 280 new customers YTD vs 1,009 — you've bought 729 fewer customers. CAC improved because you stopped buying at the margin, and the top of the funnel is now carried by organic (google/organic is the single largest source in the last 30 days, at 776 sessions and $637 of the $1,254 in revenue).
4. **Repeat mix is thickening slightly.** Returning-cohort orders were 10.5% of 2025 YTD orders (118 of 1,127) and are 14.9% now (49 of 329) — a smaller but more loyal base, which is what you'd expect when paid acquisition stops flooding in first-timers.

The honest read: this is not a CAC efficiency win you can scale from. It's the CAC you get when you turn paid off and let organic carry the load. The question worth answering next is what CAC looks like at the *margin* — i.e. what the last $5K of Google spend bought — because that's the number that tells you whether re-expanding is worth it. I can pull that by campaign type if you want it.

## Google Ads — Q1 2024 vs Q1 2026, daily basis

Live Google is dark this turn — our Google API quota is exhausted and doesn't reset until **2026-08-01 08:03 UTC**, so no live fetch is possible for any client until then. Everything below comes from the **captured store** (the dashboard's own source), which is unaffected. Coverage is `covered` for both quarters (capture floor 2022-03-05, settled through 2026-07-30), so these are complete figures and any zero is a real zero. Both are historical windows, so there's no live counterpart to show alongside them.

One basis note: these are **Google-only** pulls, so there's no store/GA revenue attached — the ROAS below is **ad-attributed** (Google's own conversionValue ÷ spend), not the dashboard card ROAS. Card ROAS can't be computed on a Google-only slice.

### Quarter totals and per-day averages

| Metric | Q1 2024 (91 days, 91 active) | Q1 2026 (90 days, 88 active) | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spend | $15,283.12 | $19,076.96 | **+24.8%** |
| **Spend / day** | **$167.95** | **$216.78** | +29.1% |
| Impressions | 1,394,631 | 5,608,479 | +302% |
| **Impr. / day** | **15,325** | **63,733** | +316% |
| Clicks | 15,526 | 126,893 | +717% |
| **Clicks / day** | **171** | **1,442** | +745% |
| CTR | 1.11% | 2.26% | +104% |
| CPC | $0.98 | $0.15 | **−85%** |
| Conversions | 465.7 | 93.8 | **−79.9%** |
| **Conv. / day** | **5.12** | **1.07** | −79.2% |
| CVR (conv/click) | 3.00% | **0.074%** | −97.5% |
| CPA | $32.82 | $203.38 | **+520%** |
| Ad-attributed value | $107,928.62 | $25,007.02 | −76.8% |
| **Value / day** | **$1,186** | **$284** | −76.1% |
| Ad ROAS | **7.06x** | **1.31x** | −81% |
| Value per click | $6.95 | $0.20 | −97% |
| Implied conv. value | $231.75 | $266.60 | +15% |

Two days in January 2026 carry no rows (88 active days vs 90 calendar). Coverage is `covered`, so those are genuinely dark days, not gaps.

### The quarters have completely different shapes

| Month | Spend | Spend/day | Clicks/day | Conv/day | CPC | Ad ROAS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 2024 | $5,800.47 | $187.11 | 198 | 4.40 | $0.95 | 5.20x |
| Feb 2024 | $3,026.52 | $104.36 | 104 | 2.92 | $1.00 | 6.95x |
| Mar 2024 | $6,456.13 | $208.26 | 205 | 7.89 | $1.01 | 8.79x |
| Jan 2026 | $752.41 | $25.94 | 448 | **0.00** | $0.06 | n/a |
| Feb 2026 | $3,186.51 | $113.80 | 1,697 | 0.78 | $0.07 | 2.18x |
| Mar 2026 | $15,138.04 | $488.32 | 2,141 | 2.33 | $0.23 | 1.19x |

Q1 2024 ran at a steady ~$100–210/day and *improved* through the quarter — March was the best month of the three on every efficiency metric (CPA $26.38, 8.79x). Q1 2026 is essentially a **March event**: 79% of the quarter's spend landed in March, ramping 20x from January's $25.94/day to $488.32/day, and efficiency **degraded** as spend scaled (ROAS 2.18x → 1.19x, CPA $146.84 → $209.96).

### What the daily numbers are actually telling you

This is not the same account doing worse — it's a different traffic mix. A $0.15 blended CPC with a 2.26% CTR and a **0.074% click-to-conversion rate** is the signature of cheap, high-volume network inventory (Display / Demand Gen / PMax display surfaces), not Search. In Q1 2024 you bought 15.5K clicks at $0.98 that converted at 3.00%. In Q1 2026 you bought 8.2x the clicks at 15% of the price and they converted at 1/40th the rate. The 745% jump in daily clicks against a 79% drop in daily conversions is the whole story.

The one thing that *held* is order size: implied conversion value per conversion is actually up 15% ($231.75 → $266.60), consistent with the ~$224 implied AOV we looked at previously. So the product economics didn't deteriorate — the acquisition efficiency did.

January 2026 is worth a hard look on its own: **12,994 clicks, $752.41 spend, exactly zero conversions.** Coverage is `covered`, so that zero is real. Nearly 13K clicks producing nothing is either a bot/low-quality placement problem or a tracking break at the start of the year — and if it's tracking, the Feb/Mar conversion figures may be understated too.

Two follow-ups I can run if useful: campaign-level splits for both quarters to name which campaign types absorbed the $19.1K in 2026, and a device + geo breakdown for Q1 2026 to test whether that click volume is real US traffic or junk placements. Say the word.

| iphone | 1.16% → **0.55%** (−53%) | $0.48 → $0.60 (+25%) | $5.59 → $3.28 (−41%) |
| android_smartphone | 1.05% → **0.52%** (−50%) | $0.38 → $0.46 (+21%) | $3.97 → $2.41 (−39%) |
| ipad | 0.73% → 0.18% (−75%) | $0.39 → $1.09 (+179%) | $2.89 → $1.93 (−33%) |
| desktop | 0.28% → 0.11% (−61%) | $1.12 → $1.80 (+61%) | $3.16 → $2.04 (−35%) |
| android_tablet | 0.62% → 0.17% | $0.26 → $1.12 | $1.60 → $1.95 |
| **Account** | **1.13% → 0.51%** | **$0.46 → $0.57** | **$5.18 → $2.90** |

Account-level context: impressions 6.64M → 2.69M (−59.5%), clicks 74,827 → 13,737 (−81.6%), conversions 1,079 → 70, CPA $31.87 → $111.14, ad-attributed ROAS 6.68x → 1.92x. *Meta conversion counts and CPA here are account-level historical figures — directionally accurate but they may not reconcile perfectly with campaign-level numbers; spend, clicks and impressions are exact.*

One limit worth knowing: the Meta **device family carries delivery metrics only** — spend, impressions, clicks. Conversions and conversion value come back as 0 on every device row in both quarters, at both device grain and in 2024 when the account was clearly converting. That is a grain limitation, not zero conversions — so **device-level ROAS/CPA cannot be computed** for either quarter.

---

## What actually changed

**1. Mix shifted off iPhone, but only modestly.** iPhone went from 82.0% → 67.5% of spend. Android smartphone picked up +10.2 pts, and tablet/desktop/other collectively went from 1.0% → 5.3%. Total mobile (iphone + android_smartphone) fell 99.0% → 94.7%. In a shrinking account that's the auction spreading Meta's now-broader delivery into surfaces it previously ignored — desktop spend actually *rose* 36% in absolute dollars while total spend fell 77%.

**2. CPMs got cheaper everywhere; clicks got more expensive everywhere.** Account CPM halved ($5.18 → $2.90) yet CPC rose 24%. That gap is entirely CTR: engagement rate roughly halved on the two devices that matter and fell harder on the long tail. You are buying more impressions per dollar and getting materially less response from them.

**3. The degradation is uniform, not device-specific.** iPhone −53% CTR, Android −50%. Nearly identical proportional decay. Whatever changed did not preferentially damage one device environment.

**On your Andromeda read:** this breakdown is consistent with it but does not by itself prove it, and I want to be straight about that. A uniform, device-agnostic CTR halving alongside collapsing CPMs is what a delivery-system change that broadens targeting looks like — audiences you built stop constraining who sees the ad, reach gets cheaper and worse. But it is *also* what budget starvation looks like: Q2 2025 spend was 23% of Q2 2024, which keeps ad sets in or near learning and degrades matching on its own. The device cut can't separate those two, because both produce the same signature here.

The cut that *would* separate them is **placement** — if the CTR loss is concentrated in Audience Network / Reels / Feed-adjacent auto-placements rather than proportional across Facebook Feed and Instagram Feed, that points at delivery expansion rather than budget. Want me to run placement for the same two quarters? I'd also pair it with `age_gender` — audience breakage should show as demographic drift away from your historical buyer profile, and budget starvation should not.

results.response:
## Meta 2024 → 2025: it wasn't a performance collapse, it was a defunding

All figures from the captured store (Meta settled through 2026-07-30, coverage `covered` for every window — the zeros below are real zeros). Meta had no spend in the current 30-day window, and these are historical periods anyway, so there's no live counterpart to show alongside. Live Google is dark right now — our Google API quota is exhausted until **2026-08-01 08:03 UTC** — but the Google figures I cite come from the captured store, which is unaffected.

### Headline

| Meta | FY2024 | FY2025 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spend | $605,487.45 | $46,767.71 | **−92.3%** |
| Impressions | 66.6M | 10.2M | −84.7% |
| Clicks | 1,039,761 | 106,305 | −89.8% |
| CTR | 1.56% | 1.04% | −33% |
| CPC | $0.58 | $0.44 | −24% (better) |
| Conversions | 13,964 | 899 | −93.6% |
| Ad-attributed value | $3,114,570.84 | $141,966.65 | −95.4% |
| **Ad ROAS** | **5.14x** | **3.04x** | −41% |

Meta conversion counts and CPA here are account-level historical figures — directionally accurate but they won't reconcile perfectly with campaign-level numbers; spend, clicks and impressions are exact.

The output fell 95%. But spend fell 92%. Efficiency fell far less than volume, and the monthly shape shows it wasn't a smooth decay — it's four distinct phases.

---

### The four phases of 2025

| 2025 | Spend | Impr. | CTR | CPC | Conv. | Ad ROAS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan | $20,743.58 | 4.67M | 1.07% | $0.41 | 470 | 2.17x |
| Feb | $5,781.57 | 979K | 1.10% | $0.54 | 129 | **4.58x** |
| Mar | $9,474.04 | 1.40M | 1.96% | $0.35 | 171 | **4.75x** |
| Apr | $5,310.64 | 1.08M | 1.16% | $0.42 | 67 | 2.68x |
| May | $1,306.83 | 966K | **0.06%** | $2.40 | 3 | **0.51x** ⚠️ |
| Jun | $1,162.60 | 642K | **0.11%** | $1.71 | 0 | — |
| Jul | $423.55 | 281K | **0.09%** | $1.69 | 0 | — |
| Aug | $647.03 | 43.5K | **2.04%** | $0.73 | 11 | **5.03x** |
| Sep | $1,917.87 | 114K | **2.72%** | $0.62 | 46 | **3.75x** |
| Oct | $0 | 0 | — | — | 2 | (late credit) |
| Nov–Dec | $0 | 0 | — | — | 0 | — |

**Phase 1 — Jan–Apr: orderly wind-down, efficiency intact.** Feb and Mar delivered 4.58x and 4.75x. That's not a broken account. It's below FY24's 5.14x blend but *well above* Aug–Oct 2024 (1.46x / 2.41x / 2.47x), which were high-spend months.

**Phase 2 — May–Jul: the actual failure.** $2,893 spent, 1.89M impressions, 1,473 clicks, **3 conversions total**. CTR fell to 0.06% and CPC quadrupled to $2.40. This is the only genuine performance breakdown in the whole year — and the placement data names the culprit.

**Phase 3 — Aug–Sep: full recovery.** 5.03x and 3.75x, at CTRs of 2.04% and 2.72% — *higher than any month in 2024* (FY24 blended CTR 1.56%). Impressions were tiny (43K, 114K), i.e. narrow controlled delivery. Whatever was rebuilt in August worked immediately.

**Phase 4 — Oct onward: dark.** Genuine $0. October's 2 conversions / $232.14 is late-attributed credit landing back on October dates from September clicks.

---

### What broke in May–Jul: Marketplace, not the audiences

Placement breakdown, both windows COMPLETE coverage (all active days carry rows):

| Placement | Nov–Dec 2024 CTR / CPC | May–Jul 2025 CTR / CPC |
|---|---|---|
| facebook:marketplace | 1.95% / **$0.20** | **0.06% / $2.41** |
| facebook:feed | 1.95% / $1.00 | 0.22% / $1.07 |
| facebook:facebook_reels | 2.30% / $0.60 | 0.11% / $1.65 |
| instagram:feed + stories + reels | $85,352 combined spend | **$10.03 combined** |

Two things jump out:

1. **Marketplace absorbed 73% of May–Jul spend** ($2,109 of $2,893) at a 0.06% CTR and a **12x higher CPC** than the same placement delivered in Nov–Dec 2024. In 2024 Marketplace was the cheap-volume workhorse — $0.20 CPC at a 1.95% CTR. In mid-2025 it became the most expensive, worst-performing inventory in the account.
2. **Instagram vanished entirely** — $85K of Instagram spend in Nov–Dec 2024 versus $10.03 across all three IG placements in May–Jul 2025. Delivery had collapsed into a single junk pool.

That is the signature of a **sub-scale budget** (~$15–20/day) with no meaningful conversion signal, where the auction dumps you into the cheapest remaining inventory and the optimizer never exits the learning phase. It is not the signature of destroyed audiences — destroyed audiences don't recover to a 2.72% CTR eight weeks later on the same ad account.

*(Nov–Dec 2024 placement list is the top 15 of 24 values by spend — a subset, not the account total. Placement rows carry no conversion attribution, so I've compared them on CTR/CPC, not ROAS.)*

---

### Where the money actually went

| FY | Meta spend | Google spend | Total ad spend |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | $605,487.45 | $34,837.01 | $640,324.46 |
| 2025 | $46,767.71 | **$302,546.35** | $349,314.06 |

Google spend rose **769%** as Meta fell 92%. This was a channel reallocation, not an abandonment of paid media.

Business-level outcome — two revenue sources, both shown:

| FY | Shopify (store) rev | Store ROAS | GA4 rev | GA4 ROAS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | $1,610,860.36 | 2.52x | $1,551,487.54 | 2.42x |
| 2025 | $1,062,971.05 | **3.04x** | $950,626.81 | 2.72x |

Store and GA4 differ because they measure different things: Shopify counts every order on order date regardless of source, while GA4 credits last-non-direct sessions it can actually attribute — so GA4 always runs a little light (−$59K in 2024, −$112K in 2025, the gap widening as more traffic went to channels GA4 tags less cleanly).

So: revenue down 34%, ad spend down 45%, **blended ROAS up from 2.52x to 3.04x**. The business got more efficient and smaller. That's a deliberate trade, not an accident.

---

### On the Andromeda thesis — the data pushes back

I know your read is that Andromeda broke the hard-won audiences and ROAS never recovered. Three findings in this dataset complicate that:

- **December 2024 was the single best month in the entire history** — 7.44x on $196,521 of spend, 6,465 conversions at a $30.40 CPA. That is *after* Andromeda's rollout began. If the audiences had been destroyed, this month shouldn't exist.
- **The efficiency soft patch predates Andromeda.** August 2024 came in at **1.46x on $34,061** — the worst high-spend month in either year — with September and October at 2.41x and 2.47x. The account was already struggling at scale in Q3 2024, then the holiday season fixed it.
- **It did recover.** August 2025 hit **5.03x** and September **3.75x**, with CTRs above anything 2024 produced. The recovery is right there in the data; it just happened at $647 and $1,918 of spend instead of $34K–$196K, so it never showed up in the annual blend.

What *is* real and worth taking seriously: the May–Jul 2025 delivery collapse was severe and it's consistent with the broader complaint that Meta's current retrieval and delivery system punishes thin budgets and sparse conversion signal far harder than it used to. A $15/day budget in 2024 would have limped; in mid-2025 it produced 3 conversions from 1.89M impressions. That's a genuine change in how the platform behaves at the low end — but it's a *scale floor* problem, not audience destruction. The fix is a minimum viable budget with consolidated signal, which is essentially what August did.

**The honest one-line answer to "what happened":** Meta didn't stop working — it got defunded by 92% in favour of Google, and the residual spend was left running below the threshold at which Meta's delivery system can function, where it dumped into Marketplace inventory at a 0.06% CTR for three months before being rebuilt in August and then switched off entirely in October.

Two things I can't answer from the data and that you flagged as outstanding earlier: **whose call the Meta pullback was**, and whether the August 2025 rebuild was a deliberate restructure or just a small test. If you can tell me the second one, I can tell you whether that 5.03x is a repeatable playbook or a fluke on 11 conversions.

## Shopify — November 2025 vs November 2024

Both windows are fully covered (Shopify capture floor 2022-01-24, settled through 2026-07-30, refund-adjusted), so these are complete figures, not partials. Revenue basis is **net sales** — after discounts and refunds, excluding shipping and tax.

| Metric | Nov 2025 | Nov 2024 | Δ | Δ% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Orders** | 777 | 1,612 | −835 | **−51.8%** |
| **Units** | 1,093 | 2,347 | −1,254 | **−53.4%** |
| **Net sales** | $169,946.96 | $361,504.79 | −$191,557.83 | **−53.0%** |
| **AOV** | $218.72 | $224.26 | −$5.54 | **−2.5%** |
| Units / order | 1.41 | 1.46 | −0.05 | −3.4% |
| Revenue / unit | $155.49 | $154.03 | +$1.46 | +0.9% |
| Distinct product rows | 159 | 227 | −68 | −30.0% |

Units come from the product grain; product revenue reconciles exactly to the account total in both windows ($169,946.96 / $361,504.79), so the unit counts are sound. Note that product-grain revenue ÷ units is $155.49 — that's revenue per unit, **not** AOV. AOV uses distinct orders.

## The money waterfall

| Component | Nov 2025 | Nov 2024 | Δ% |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gross sales | $175,100.00 | $370,105.00 | −52.7% |
| − Discounts | $3,684.04 | $5,880.21 | −37.3% |
| = Net sales | $169,946.96 | $361,504.79 | −53.0% |
| + Taxes | $3,279.28 | $8,043.38 | −59.2% |
| + Shipping | $225.00 | $825.00 | −72.7% |
| = Total sales | $173,451.24 | $370,373.17 | −53.2% |
| Refunds | $796.13 | $2,012.51 | −60.4% |

Fees and the tax sub-components (discount tax, cart tax, shipping tax) were not captured on any day in either window — that's "not captured," not $0, so I can't give you a contribution-margin view from this.

## What the comparison actually says

**This is a pure volume collapse, not a pricing or mix problem.** AOV held within 2.5% and revenue per unit actually rose slightly (+0.9%). Basket depth barely moved (1.41 vs 1.46 units/order). Every dollar of the $191.6K gap is fewer orders — 835 of them.

**Discounting got deeper on less volume.** Discounts fell 37.3% in absolute terms but rose as a share of gross, from 1.59% to 2.10%. You spent proportionally more margin per dollar sold and still lost half the orders.

**Refund quality improved slightly** — 0.45% of gross vs 0.54%. Not a returns problem.

**Assortment narrowed by 30%** — 159 product rows vs 227. Fewer SKUs transacting, though the ones that did sell held their price.

**The obvious context:** Nov 2024 sat on top of ~$153K of Meta spend at 4.26x. Meta was completely dark in Q4 2025 ($0 spend, genuine zero). A 52% order decline against the removal of six figures of monthly paid demand is the shape you'd expect — the store didn't get worse at converting or monetizing, it got much smaller top-of-funnel. If you want, I can pull November's Google spend for both years and put a blended MER on each side so the comparison is efficiency-adjusted rather than just volume-adjusted.

## Shopify revenue — Nov–Dec 2025 vs Nov–Dec 2024

From the captured store, settled through 2026-07-30. Coverage is `covered` for Shopify (and Google, Meta, GA) across both windows with a capture floor of 2022-01-24 — both figures are complete, not partials. These are historical windows, so there's no live snapshot to show alongside them (live only spans the last 30 days). Google figures below also come from the captured store — live Google is dark platform-wide right now because our API quota is exhausted until 2026-08-01 08:03 UTC.

| Shopify (store card) | Nov–Dec 2025 | Nov–Dec 2024 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Revenue** | **$677,248.35** | **$997,108.83** | **−$319,860.48 (−32.1%)** |
| Orders | 3,006 | 4,498 | −1,492 (−33.2%) |
| AOV | $225.30 | $221.68 | +$3.62 (+1.6%) |

**The drop is entirely an order-count story, not a basket story.** AOV actually ticked *up* 1.6%. You lost ~1,492 orders; had AOV been flat at 2024 levels, the revenue gap would be almost identical. Nothing degraded about what buyers did once they bought — there were just a third fewer of them.

### What changed on the paid side

| Ad spend | Nov–Dec 2025 | Nov–Dec 2024 |
|---|---|---|
| Meta | **$0.00** | $349,653.78 |
| Google | $173,122.67 | $4,509.25 |
| **Total** | **$173,122.67** | **$354,163.03** (−51.1%) |
| **Blended MER (store rev ÷ spend)** | **3.91x** | **2.82x** |

Complete channel inversion. Holiday 2024 was a Meta-funded quarter with Google as a rounding error; holiday 2025 was Google-only with Meta at a genuine zero (coverage `covered`, so that $0 is real — Meta was dark, not unmeasured).

**Revenue fell 32% while spend fell 51%.** On a blended basis you bought $677K of store revenue for $173K, versus $997K for $354K — MER improved from 2.82x to 3.91x. That's ~$147K more gross contribution-before-COGS in 2025 despite the smaller top line. This period was less productive in absolute revenue but materially more *efficient*.

### Second revenue source — GA4

Both windows carry a GA-measured revenue figure alongside Shopify, and they disagree:

| Source | Nov–Dec 2025 | MER | Nov–Dec 2024 | MER |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shopify (store, card figure) | $677,248.35 | 3.91x | $997,108.83 | 2.82x |
| GA4 | $599,847.83 | 3.46x | $865,810.60 | 2.44x |

GA4 runs 11–13% below Shopify in both periods. That's expected and consistent: Shopify is the order of record (every order, refund-adjusted on its own `updated_at` basis), while GA4 only counts purchases it could tie to a tracked session — consent/cookie loss, ad-blocking, cross-device and app-browser sessions, and Safari ITP all shave transactions off the GA side. GA also credits on session/click date rather than order date. The gap being stable across both years is the good news — it means the measurement basis didn't shift between them, so the year-over-year comparison holds on either source.

### On the Andromeda read

Worth being precise here, because the data pushes back a little on the framing. This particular comparison isn't a story of Meta running and delivering worse ROAS — Meta spend in Nov–Dec 2025 was **exactly zero**. So the −32% cannot be attributed to Andromeda degrading audience performance in this window; there was no Meta delivery to degrade. What it shows is the revenue consequence of *not being on Meta at all* during the peak season, partially offset by Google scaling from $4.5K to $173K. The Andromeda thesis would have to be tested in the periods where Meta was actually spending — Q1–Q3 2025 — not here.

Want me to break these two periods out by month, or look at whether the lost orders show up as a specific channel gap in GA (i.e. did Google + organic actually backfill Meta's former demand, or did paid social traffic simply vanish)?

Meta's zeros are real: coverage is `covered` and capture is healthy, so Meta was genuinely dark across both 56 days. Google's prior 28 days are a confirmed real $0; the rolling 28 days show $0 across the 27 captured days, with Jul 31 unconfirmed.

**Consequence:** ROAS, MER, CPA, CPC and CTR cannot be computed for either window — the denominator is zero. Not "0x", not "down 100%" — undefined. Every dollar of revenue below is unpaid demand. Meta conversion counts here are account-level historical figures — directionally accurate, may not perfectly reconcile with campaign-level numbers; Meta spend/clicks/impressions are exact.

---

## 2. Shopify — the store improved on flat volume

| Metric | Rolling 28d | Prior 28d | Δ |

| **Net sales** (excl. shipping & tax) | **$1,508.00** | **$1,337.00** | **+$171.00 (+12.8%)** |
| Total sales | $1,598.54 | $1,337.00 | +$261.54 (+19.6%) |
| **Orders** | **8** | **8** | **flat** |
| **AOV** | **$188.50** | $167.13 | **+$21.37 (+12.8%)** |
| Gross sales | $1,523.00 | $1,337.00 | +$186.00 |
| Discounts | $15.00 | $0.00 | +$15.00 |
| Shipping collected | $75.00 | $0.00 | +$75.00 |
| Taxes | $15.54 | $0.00 | +$15.54 |
| Refunds | $0.00 | $0.00 | flat (0% both) |

Coverage on both money windows is complete (27/27 and 28/28 sale days). `fees` is **not captured** on any day in either window — that's "not captured," not $0, so contribution margin can't be closed out from this data.

The genuinely notable line is the prior window: **$0 shipping and $0 tax across all 8 orders** versus $75 shipping and $15.54 tax on the current 8. Same order count, same store, materially different checkout composition — worth confirming whether a free-shipping promo or a tax-exemption/nexus setting was live in June.

Entire lift is **AOV, not volume**: 8 orders both periods. Basket mix drove it (the $1,016 Castle Sofa line plus cover-set/personalization add-ons).

---

## 3. GA4 — revenue nearly doubled while event conversions fell a third

| Metric | Rolling 28d | Prior 28d | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GA4 revenue** | **$1,254.00** | **$636.00** | **+$618.00 (+97.2%)** |
| **GA4 conversions** (all conversion events) | **151** | **228** | **−77 (−33.8%)** |
| Implied value per conversion event | $8.30 | $2.79 | +$5.51 |

These move in opposite directions, and the channel split says why:

| GA4 channel | Rolling 28d rev | Prior 28d rev | Rolling conv | Prior conv |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Organic Search** | **$891** | $144 | 80 | 87 |
| **Direct** | $363 | **$648** | 53 | 89 |
| Referral | $0 | $49 | **2** | **40** |
| Unassigned | $0 | $49 | 30 | 6 |
| Organic Shopping (free listings) | $0 | $0 | 8 | 7 |
| Organic Social | $0 | $0 | 2 | 10 |
| Paid Search / Paid Social | $0 | $0 | 0 | 0 |

Channel coverage verdict: **COMPLETE** for both windows — no caveat needed on this ranking.

- **Organic Search is the whole revenue story:** $144 → $891 (+518%). It overtook Direct as the top revenue channel.
- **Direct lost both revenue (−44%) and conversions (−40%)** — the single biggest drag on the event count.
- **Referral collapsed: 40 conversions → 2.** In the prior window referral (Facebook-sourced sessions) was a real assisted-conversion contributor; it has essentially stopped converting. With Meta dark for 56 straight days, the residual organic Facebook referral traffic has decayed — that's the mechanism, and it's a paid-media absence effect, not a Meta targeting/audience effect (there is no delivery to break).
- **Unassigned jumped 6 → 30 conversions**, so part of the Direct/Referral conversion decline is reattribution noise rather than pure loss. Don't read the −33.8% as a clean demand drop.
- **Paid Search shows 0 revenue and 0 conversions in both windows** — consistent with $0 Google spend.

## 4. Live vs captured — they disagree, and here's why

Both sources exist for Shopify and GA4, so both get reported:

| | Store revenue | Orders |
|---|---|---|
| **LIVE panel** (provisional as of 2026-08-01 04:38Z, 30-day window Jul 2–31) | $1,254.00 net sales | 7 |
| **CAPTURED** (settled through 2026-07-30, 28-day window Jul 4–31) | $1,508.00 net sales | 8 |

That's one order / $254 of difference. Two reasons, both expected: the windows differ (live spans 30 days, captured 28), and captured Shopify is **change-based on `updated_at` and refund-adjusted as of its last re-sum**, whereas live is a provisional snapshot. An order whose status/total moved gets credited differently between them. Captured wins on overlap once settled. I'm not blending them.

GA4 agrees across sources at **$1,254** — and note the live panel reports a **$0.00 GA4-vs-Shopify delta on its own 30-day basis**, while on the captured 28-day basis the store sits **$254 above GA4**. Same reason: settlement and window, not a tracking break.

---

## 5. What I'd take from this

1. **There is no paid-media comparison to make.** 56 consecutive days of zero spend on both platforms. Any ROAS/MER conversation is on hold until spend resumes — and the Andromeda thesis can't be tested on this window at all, because nothing was delivered.
2. **Organic Search is carrying the business right now** and it's improving fast ($144 → $891). Landing-page data shows `/` converting at 4.63% and `/products/foamoh-original-play-castle-sofa` at only 0.84% on 119 sessions — the PDP is the leak, not traffic.
3. **AOV is up 12.8% on flat 8 orders.** Volume is the constraint. Nothing in the funnel is broken; there's simply no top-of-funnel spend.
4. **Two things to verify off-platform:** the June $0 shipping/$0 tax condition (promo or settings?), and Shopify `fees` capture, which is missing entirely and blocks any margin view.

Want me to pull Google's last non-zero spend month to pin exactly when the account went dark, or dig into the PDP conversion gap?

## Short answer: no — it will still move, and one day of it isn't even in yet.

**The two numbers on the table (never blended):**

| Source | Basis | Conversions |
|---|---|---|
| **Live snapshot** (GA4 panel) | provisional, as-of **2026-08-01 04:44Z** | **89.0** conversions / 2 purchases / $363.00 |
| **Captured store** | settled through **2026-07-30** | **54** conversions across all platforms, $363.00 canonical revenue (store basis) |

Those aren't in conflict — they're different settlement points. Live is intraday and unsettled; captured is the dashboard's own source and stops at 7/30.

---

## Why it will move

**1. Day 7 is missing from the captured side.** I ran 7/25→7/31 and 7/25→7/30 separately and they return *identical* totals (54 conversions, 24 rows). That means **zero rows exist for July 31**. Capture is settled through 2026-07-30, and Google capture has been **failing since 2026-07-31 17:36 UTC** — so any Google contribution to 7/31 is uncaptured, not $0 and not disconnected. Your "last 7 days" captured figure is really 6 days right now. (Separately, live Google is dark for every client because our Google API quota is exhausted until **2026-08-01 08:03 UTC** — that's an outage on our side, not the account.)

**2. GA4 restates for 7 days.** GA4 processing takes 24–48h and the numbers *change during it*, and intraday carries gaps in event-scoped source dimensions plus extra "(other)" rows. So 7/29–7/31 in particular are soft. The 89 will land somewhere else — expect it to be broadly stable around **~Aug 7**.

**3. Meta restates 9 days minimum** (1-day/7-day attribution), 28 days if a 28-day window is in use. Meta had **no spend** in this window, so there's nothing to re-credit from live activity — but late-attributed credit can still land on zero-spend dates (we saw exactly that in Q4 2025, $232.14 of value against $0 spend). Low risk, non-zero.

**4. Google conversions are credited to click date.** As conversion lag settles, conversions get written *backwards* onto days already in the window. Captured Google spend for 7/25–7/30 is a genuine $0 (status ok), so there's little ad-driven lag to catch up — but the 7/31 gap has to be filled before that's a clean statement.

**5. Shopify has no settlement window at all.** It's change-based on `updated_at`, so a refund months or years from now still moves the order and revenue side. Right now it's 2 orders, 0 refunds, $363.00 net — clean, but never technically "final."

---

## Practical read

- **Revenue side is about as firm as it gets:** Shopify $363.00 (canonical, store basis) and GA4 $363.00 agree to the dollar on 2 orders / 2 transactions. Both would only move on a refund.
- **The conversion count is the soft one** — it's mostly GA4 micro-conversions (60 add_to_cart, 24 begin_checkout, 3 add_payment_info, 2 purchase), and those are exactly the events GA4 reprocesses. Only the **2 purchases** should be treated as hard.
- **If you need a number you can publish**, use the window ending **2026-07-24** or earlier, or wait until ~Aug 7 for GA4 and ~Aug 9 for Meta.

One caveat on the captured figure: Meta conversion counts and CPA are account-level historical figures — directionally accurate, but they may not reconcile perfectly with campaign-level conversion numbers. Meta spend, clicks and impressions are exact.

I'd also flag the Google capture failure as an ops item — it's been down since yesterday afternoon and every "last 7 days" total will read understated on the Google side until it's restarted.

## December — with November a very close second, and the answer flips depending on which revenue source you use

All figures below come from the **captured store** (settled through 2026-07-30), not the live feed. Live Google is dark right now: our Google API quota is exhausted and doesn't reset until **2026-08-01 08:03 UTC**, so nothing Google-related can be fetched live for any client until then. Coverage is `covered` for every month below, so the zeros are real zeros. Two exceptions I'll name up front:

- **Jan–Feb 2022** are excluded — Google capture starts 2022-03-05, so those months can't be assessed.
- **Meta predates capture before 2023-06-21** — we have no captured Meta data before that date, so 2022 and early-2023 spend/ROAS is Google-only (not $0 for Meta, just uncaptured).
- **Jul 2026** — Google capture is currently failing (last captured 2026-07-30), so that month's Google side is understated. Immaterial here since Google spend was $0 all month anyway.

---

## Seasonality by calendar month — Shopify (store) revenue, all years pooled

| Month | Total (all yrs) | Avg / yr | Yrs | Best single year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Dec** | **$1,263,301** | **$315,825** | 4 | Dec '24 — $635,604 |
| **Nov** | **$1,165,098** | **$291,275** | 4 | Nov '23 — $582,885 |
| Sep | $364,865 | $91,216 | 4 | Sep '23 — $163,214 |
| Aug | $290,413 | $72,603 | 4 | Aug '23 — $169,868 |
| Jul | $215,395 | $43,079 | 5 | Jul '23 — $109,359 |
| Oct | $166,124 | $41,531 | 4 | Oct '24 — $72,541 |
| Mar | $153,145 | $30,629 | 5 | Mar '24 — $96,130 |
| May | $115,444 | $23,089 | 5 | May '24 — $49,785 |
| Jan | $111,485 | $27,871 | 4 | Jan '24 — $63,947 |
| Jun | $102,876 | $20,575 | 5 | Jun '25 — $54,965 |
| Feb | $75,833 | $18,958 | 4 | Feb '24 — $33,447 |
| Apr | $73,937 | $14,787 | 5 | Apr '24 — $50,232 |

**December wins on every store-basis test:** highest pooled total, highest per-year average, and it was the single strongest month of its own year in **3 of the 4 complete years** (2022, 2024, 2025). November took 2023.

---

## The basis matters — GA4 flips the order

Both revenue sources are present in every one of these windows, and they disagree:

| | Store (Shopify) | GA4 |
|---|---|---|
| **November, all yrs** | $1,165,098 | **$1,198,530** |
| **December, all yrs** | **$1,263,301** | $1,115,733 |

So on **Shopify order-date revenue December is strongest; on GA4 session-attributed revenue November is strongest**, by about 7%. The gap comes almost entirely from 2023: GA4 booked $669,489 in Nov '23 against Shopify's $582,885, and only $58,402 in Dec '23 against Shopify's $47,464. GA4 credits revenue to the session that drove it (client-side, campaign-attributed, no refund adjustment), while Shopify counts the order when it's placed and nets refunds — so a late-November click converting into a December order lands in different months on the two systems. Shopify is the card figure and the one I'd anchor to; GA4 is the useful cross-check.

---

## What actually makes Q4 the season

**Dec + Nov combined share of annual store revenue:**
- 2023: 54.2% ($631K of $1.164M) — but almost all of it *November*
- 2024: 61.9% ($997K of $1.611M)
- 2025: 63.7% ($677K of $1.063M)

Two-thirds of the year lands in eight weeks. And December isn't just volume — it's the best-priced month too: AOV hit **$52.15 in Dec '24** and $47.26 in Dec '22, against a mid-year norm in the $23–33 range.

Efficiency holds up in December as well (store revenue ÷ total ad spend): **6.71x Dec '22, 5.39x Dec '23, 3.21x Dec '24, 3.75x Dec '25**. November: 5.22x / 5.72x / 2.32x / 4.50x. So December is the stronger month on both volume *and* return — the 2024 dip to 3.21x is the $198K Meta-heavy spend month, not a demand problem.

**The 2023 anomaly is worth understanding before you plan off this.** Nov '23 was the single largest November ($582,885 store / $669,489 GA4) on $100,913 of Meta spend — then Meta spend collapsed to $7,744 in December and December revenue fell to $47,464. That's the one year December wasn't the peak, and it looks like a spend decision, not seasonality.

**Historically weakest: April** ($14,787/yr avg), then February and June.

One caution on extrapolating: 2026 is running well below every prior year — Apr $5,100, May $3,752, Jun $1,054, Jul $1,826, with **zero captured ad spend on either platform since May 1**. The seasonal *shape* above is solid across four years, but the *level* it would scale from this year is a fraction of 2024/2025.

## Google / Meta spend split — 2024 → now

Live Google is dark this turn (our Google API quota is exhausted platform-wide until **2026-08-01 08:03 UTC** — that's an outage on our side, not a fact about the account), so every figure below comes from the **captured store**, settled through 2026-07-30. That's the same source the dashboard cards read.

| Period | Meta spend | Google spend | Total | Split (Meta / Google) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **FY2024** | $605,487.45 | $34,837.01 | $640,324.46 | **94.6% / 5.4%** |
| **FY2025** | $46,767.71 | $302,546.35 | $349,314.06 | **13.4% / 86.6%** |

⚠️ The 2026 YTD Google figure is **partial** — Google capture has been failing since 2026-07-31, so 2026-07-31 is not in the store. Everything through 07-30 is captured; that missing day is not $0 and not a disconnect, just uncaptured.

---

## The shift is a full channel inversion, then a shutdown

**2024 — Meta-dominant.** Meta outspent Google **17.4 : 1**. Q4 2024 alone was $387,951.78 on Meta at 5.69x ad-attributed ROAS. Google was a rounding error at $34.8K for the year (the 29.82x FY24 Google ROAS is the same conversion-tracking inflation we've flagged before — don't quote it).

**2025 — inverted.** Meta collapsed to $46.8K (−92% YoY) while Google scaled to $302.5K (+769% YoY). Google went from 5% of budget to 87%. On a like-for-like ad-attributed basis the two channels ended up nearly identical in efficiency that year: **Meta 3.04x vs Google 2.89x** — so the reallocation didn't buy better measured efficiency, it bought scale on a channel that could absorb it.

**2025→2026 — both channels went dark, in sequence.**

| Month 2026 | Google spend |
|---|---|
| Jan | $752.41 |
| Feb | $3,186.51 |
| Mar | $15,138.04 |
| Apr | $3,230.89 (concentrated in the first few days) |
| May | $0.00 |
| Jun | $0.00 |
| Jul | $0.00 (through 07-30) |

- **Last Meta spend: September 2025.** Q3 2025 was $2,988.45; Q4 2025 was a genuine $0 (coverage `covered`) with $232.14 of late-attributed value landing on Q4 dates from Q3 clicks. Meta has been at $0 every month since — Q1, Q2 and July 2026 all confirmed zero.
- **Last Google spend: early April 2026.** March was the 2026 peak at $15,138.04, then April cut off after a few days and May onward is $0.

So the "split" question has an uncomfortable answer: **there is no split anymore.** From May 2026 forward, captured paid spend across both channels is $0.00. The current 30-day window (Jul 2–31) has zero paid media on either platform — live Meta agrees with captured here ($0 both sides), and captured Google confirms $0 through 07-30. The $1,254.00 in Shopify net sales and 7 orders this month are running entirely on organic and direct (776 google/organic + 703 direct sessions).

**Two things worth your attention:**

1. **2026 Google efficiency was materially worse than 2025** — 1.29x ad-attributed for the year vs 2.89x in 2025, with CPA at $203.35 vs $77.54. Impressions held up (6.3M on $22K, CPC $0.16) but that's cheap Display/PMax-style inventory, not the $1.91-CPC search volume that drove 2025. Spend split: Google $51,166.07, Meta $7,780.07.

---

## Why they disagree

**1. Different measurement basis (the structural reason).** Shopify net sales = gross − discounts, refund-adjusted, **excluding shipping and tax**. GA4 `purchase` revenue is whatever value the datalayer pushed at checkout — it is not recomputed and not refund-adjusted unless refund events are explicitly sent. Q2's store waterfall:

| Component | Q2 2025 |
|---|---|
| Gross sales | $121,067.00 |
| Discounts | −$1,993.00 |
| Refunds | −$364.00 |
| **Net sales** | **$117,840.00** |
| Taxes (+) | $2,538.24 |
| Shipping (+) | $150.00 |
| Tips (+) | $0.00 |
| **Total sales** | **$120,528.24** |

Note $117,840 is the settled net the store reports; gross − discounts − refunds leaves ~$1.2K unaccounted, which is on-sale markdown / line-level adjustment inside the store's own net calculation. Also: **fees, cart tax and shipping tax were not captured on any of the 91 days** — that's "not captured", not $0.

**2. GA4 is a one-way undercount, which matches the direction.** GA4 loses purchases to consent denial, ad blockers, and express/accelerated checkouts (Shop Pay, PayPal) where the thank-you page tag doesn't fire — plus draft, POS and manually-created orders never generate a GA4 event at all. Shopify sees every order; GA4 only sees the ones that fired a tag. A ~2% shortfall is exactly the size of that leakage, not a bug.

**3. Date/timezone credit.** Shopify credits by order `created_at` in store timezone; GA4 by event timestamp in property timezone. Orders near midnight on 2025-03-31 and 2025-06-30 land on different sides of the quarter boundary in each system.

**4. Restatement direction differs.** Shopify's captured figure is change-based on `updated_at` — a refund logged in 2026 still moves Q2 2025 downward on the next re-sum. GA4 restates only a 7-day trailing window and then freezes, so a Q2 refund never reduces the GA4 number.

**5. The ad-attributed $162K is a third basis entirely** — click-date credit inside Google's and Meta's own conversion windows, with cross-platform overlap. It's 38% above actual store revenue and should never be reconciled against the other two as like-for-like.

---

## Worth noting

In the current window (July 2026) GA4 and Shopify are at **exact parity — $1,254.00 vs $1,254.00, 7 transactions vs 7 orders, $0.00 delta**. So whatever tagging leakage produced the Q2 2025 gap looks to have been closed since — though with only 7 orders in the current window that's a small sample to draw a trend from.

For footnoting: use **$117,840 / 2.00x** as the Q2 2025 headline (that's the dashboard card figure), and footnote GA4's $115,634.87 as "site-analytics basis, 1.9% tag-loss shortfall."

Both figures below are from the **captured store** (settled through 2026-07-30, coverage `covered` on Meta, Shopify, Google and GA — so these are complete, not partial). | **Shopify orders** | **559** | $117,840 (card revenue) | $210.81 |
| Gap | **−489 orders (−87.5%)** | −$102,926 | +$2.24 (+1.1%) |

Meta claims **12.5% of Q2 orders**.

---

### 1. First — don't sum Meta's purchase rows. There's a nasty coincidence here.
Meta reports the same purchase event under 8 alias action types, each showing **70**: `purchase`, `omni_purchase`, `offsite_conversion.fb_pixel_purchase`, `onsite_web_purchase`, `onsite_web_app_purchase`, `web_in_store_purchase`, `web_app_in_store_purchase`, `offsite_purchase_add_20_s_calls`. Sum them naively and you get **560** — which sits 1 order away from Shopify's 559 and looks like a perfect reconciliation. It is pure arithmetic accident. The real Meta purchase count is **70**, and the $14,913.50 value ties exactly to Meta's account-level conversion value for the quarter, which confirms the dedupe.

### 2. The value basis is *not* the problem — volume is
Per-purchase value is $213.05 (Meta) vs $210.81 (Shopify), a 1.1% difference. That tells you the pixel is passing an order value consistent with what Shopify books, so you can rule out a shipping/tax/discount basis mismatch as the driver. The entire 489-order gap is attribution scope, not measurement of the money.

### 3. Why the 489-order gap exists
- **Meta only counts ad-touched orders.** It's a subset by construction — 489 orders had no qualifying Meta impression or click. Meta spend was $7,780.07 of $58,946.14 total Q2 spend (13.2%), so claiming 12.5% of orders is roughly proportional to its share of budget. Google carried the quarter at $51,166.07.
- **Date basis differs.** Meta credits the purchase back to the date of the ad impression/click; Shopify books it on order-created date. That shifts a handful of orders across the Apr 1 and Jun 30 boundaries in both directions (March clicks → April orders land in March on Meta; June clicks → July orders land in June).
- **Attribution window.** Meta's default 7-day-click / 1-day-view can only capture purchases inside that lookback. For a $200+ considered purchase like the Castle Sofa, longer consideration cycles fall outside it entirely.
- **Shopify is refund-adjusted and channel-agnostic.** It includes organic, direct, email, bing, repeat customers — Q2 monthly orders were Apr 72, May 222, Jun 265.

### 4. The bigger reconciliation problem is cross-platform, not Meta-vs-Shopify
Meta's claimed value ($14,913.50) plus Google's claimed value ($147,364.67) = **$162,278.17**, which is **138% of the $117,840 the store actually recorded**. Google alone claims $29.5K more revenue than the entire store took in. So the platform-claimed values cannot be added — and Google is the source of the inflation, consistent with the tracking anomaly we've flagged on this account before. GA4 is the sane third read: $115,634.87 for Q2, within 1.9% of Shopify.

Blended reality for Q2: **$117,840 store revenue ÷ $58,946.14 spend = 2.00x**. Meta's own 1.92x ad ROAS ($14,913.50 ÷ $7,780.07) happens to land close to blended, but on a different basis.

One caveat on the Meta side: these are Meta account-level historical figures — directionally accurate but they may not reconcile perfectly against campaign-level conversion numbers. Meta spend, clicks and impressions are exact.

If you want, I can pull the Meta purchase count month-by-month for Q2 to see whether the 70 clusters against the April spend or trails off as spend wound down toward the Q4 blackout.

## Q2 2025 (Apr 1 – Jun 30) — the best full-funnel path

First, the honest structural caveat: **there is no single joined campaign → landing page → creative row in the data.** GA4 gives me campaign → landing page. Meta gives me creative assets, but its asset rows carry zero conversions/revenue (component attribution, not a partition). Google's creative equivalent — PMax asset groups — isn't a captured family at all. So the path below is *stitched* from two overlapping datasets, and I'll mark where each leg is evidence vs. inference.

Also: all Google figures come from the **captured store**, not the live feed — our Google API quota is exhausted and doesn't reset until **2026-08-01 08:03 UTC**. The captured store is unaffected and is what the dashboard reads. My first campaign-grain call timed out; the retry returned platform rollups (137 Google campaign rows, 180 Meta rows aggregated), not per-campaign lines — so campaign *naming* below comes from GA4's campaign dimension, not from Google's own spend rows.

---

## The winning path: Sales-Performance Max-Evergreen → Castle Sofa PDP → Original Play Castle Sofa™️

**Leg 1 — Campaign (GA4-attributed revenue, Q2 2025):**

| Campaign | GA4 revenue | Share of paid |
|---|---|---|
| **Sales-Performance Max-Evergreen** | **$52,757** | 99.4% of all `google / cpc` revenue |
| Meta (fb/paid + facebook/paid + ig/paid) | $3,791.54 | — |
| Sales-Search-8 | $324 | — |

`google / cpc` totals $53,081 in GA4 for the quarter, and PMax Evergreen accounts for $52,757 of it. Search contributed $324. This wasn't a portfolio — it was one campaign.

**The two ROAS bases disagree sharply and you need both:**
- **Ad-attributed (Google's own conversion value ÷ spend):** $147,364.66 / $51,166.07 = **2.88x**
- **GA4-attributed (`google / cpc` revenue ÷ all Google spend):** $53,081 / $51,166.07 = **1.04x**

That's a ~2.8x gap. It's the same pattern flagged in earlier work on this account: Google's value counts view-through and long-window PMax credit and fires on its own conversion actions, while GA4 credits last non-direct click on order date. Neither is wrong; the honest read is that PMax was roughly **break-even to slightly profitable on a GA4 basis** and looked strongly profitable on Google's basis. Note also `(direct) / (none)` carried $38,899 — a large chunk of which is almost certainly PMax demand landing as direct.

**Leg 2 — Landing page.** Coverage on GA4 landing pages is COMPLETE for all 91 days. Two surfaces did the work:

| Landing surface | GA4 revenue (Q2) |
|---|---|
| `/` (homepage, clean) | $14,649.54 |
| `/products/foamoh-original-play-castle-sofa` (clean) | $7,719 |
| Castle Sofa PDP — Google-tagged variants (`tw_source=google`, `gad_campaignid=20382323183`) | ~$20,290 across 6 rows |
| Homepage — Google-tagged variants | ~$8,899 across 2 rows |
| `/collections/all` — Google-tagged | ~$3,549 |
| `/products/foamoh-super-castle-play-sofa` | $3,415 |

**The Original Play Castle Sofa PDP is the highest-revenue paid landing surface** once you consolidate its tagged variants (~$28K including the clean row) — ahead of the homepage (~$23.5K consolidated). That's the strongest single finding here: paid traffic monetizes better landing on the Castle Sofa PDP than on `/`.

One caveat on that table: GA4's "conversions" in this breakdown counts *all* conversion events (add_to_cart, begin_checkout, purchase), so the derived per-row AOV ($9–$19) is not an order value — ignore it. The revenue column is the reliable signal.

The `/products/foamoh-super-castle-play-sofa` rows are the interesting outlier — $3,415 on only 79 events, an implied value-per-event 2–4x every other page. Low volume, premium SKU, materially better economics per session. That's an untested scaling lane.

**Leg 3 — Creative. This is where the path breaks, and I won't fake it.**

The creative leg exists **only on Meta** — and Meta was *not* the winning channel in Q2. $7,780.07 spend, 69 conversions, $14,679.50 ad-attributed value (**1.89x**), against just $3,791.54 of GA4-attributed paid-social revenue (**~0.49x on a GA4 basis**). Meta account-level conversion counts and CPA are directionally accurate but may not reconcile perfectly with campaign-grain numbers; Meta spend, clicks and impressions are exact.

So I can't hand you "the winning creative in the winning path" — the winning path ran on PMax, and PMax asset-group creative isn't captured. What I *can* give you is the Meta creative ranking (asset spend is component attribution, over/under the ad total by design — compare within type only, never sum across types):

| Video asset | Spend | Impr. | CTR | CPC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Stop motion 2 vertical.mov** | $1,677.16 | 382,817 | **1.37%** | **$0.32** |
| cropped_1X1 … META 4:5 Stop motion 2 vertical | $1,115.22 | 62,458 | **2.69%** | $0.66 |
| cropped_1X1 (360,0) 2160px **Stop motion 2.mov** | **$2,675.91** | 1,919,712 | **0.05%** | **$2.67** |
| cropped_1X1 Red Square.mov | $486.35 | 20,162 | 2.12% | $1.14 |
| cropped_1X1 Pink Castle Vertical.mov | $323.03 | 17,358 | 1.85% | $1.01 |

Image: `untitled_105` — $624.83, 123,847 impr, **2.84% CTR, $0.18 CPC**, the cheapest clicks of anything in the account that quarter.

**The clear creative story:** the *Stop motion 2* concept works, and the **vertical cut** is the winner — 1.37% CTR at $0.32 CPC, and its 1:1 crop of the 4:5 vertical hit 2.69% CTR. Meanwhile the **square 2160px crop of the same source video burned $2,675.91 — 34% of all Meta spend — at 0.05% CTR and $2.67 CPC** across 1.9M impressions. That's not a creative failure, it's a placement/format failure: 1.9M impressions at that CTR is cheap reach inventory, and the square crop was the asset feeding it.

---

## Bottom line

- **Best evidenced full-funnel path:** `Sales-Performance Max-Evergreen` → **Original Play Castle Sofa PDP** (~$28K GA4 revenue consolidated across tagged variants, beating the homepage) → **FoamOh Original Play Castle Sofa™️**. GA4-basis ROAS ~1.04x; Google-basis 2.88x — footnote both.
- **Best creative combination:** *Stop motion 2, vertical cut* + the `untitled_105` image, on feed/reels placements. But this sits on the Meta side, which returned 0.49x on a GA4 basis — so it's the best creative in the *weaker* channel, not part of the winning path.
- **The gap you should close:** you can't currently tie creative to the path that actually made money, because PMax asset-group performance isn't captured. If proving creative→revenue matters for Q2 retrospectives, that's a data-collection change, not an analysis one.
- **Most under-exploited lane:** the Super Castle Play Sofa PDP — 2–4x the value-per-event of every other landing page on trivial volume.

## What the Q4 record actually says

**1. AOV is the one constant.** $214–$226 across four years, four totally different media mixes. That is your safest planning input.

**2. The Meta-dark quarter was the *more efficient* quarter.** Q4 2024 spent $393K (98.7% Meta) and returned 2.72x. Q4 2025 spent $183K (100% Google) and returned **3.84x**. The planning consequence: you will be restarting a smart-bidding Google account that has been off for **five months** going into the highest-CPC quarter of the year. That relearning cost is the single biggest risk to the number, and it has to be paid in October — which is also the quarter's least efficient window. That's inconvenient but it's the right place to spend it.

# Part 3 — Q4 2026 plan

Calendar anchors: Black Friday **Fri 27 Nov 2026**, Cyber Monday **Mon 30 Nov 2026** — one week later than 2025, which compresses the December runway by ~7 days.

## Budget scenarios

| | A — Rebuild | **B — Base (recommended)** | C — Reopen Meta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Google spend | $120,000 | **$185,000** | $185,000 |
| Meta spend | $0 | **$0** | $60,000 (capped test) |

It lands ~8% below Q4 2025 revenue on identical spend — that is the honest number, not a growth story, and I'd rather you carry it into the client meeting than a 3.84x repeat.

Scenario C only makes sense if Meta is funded as a **capped incrementality test**, not a scaling play. The 2024 marginal was $1.75; assume Meta returns 1.5–2.0x until proven otherwise. Kill rule: if Meta store-attributable ROAS is under 2.0x by Nov 15, it doesn't run through BFCM.

## Phasing (Scenario B, $185K)

| Window | Dates | Spend | % | Target rev | Target ROAS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ramp / relearn** | Oct 1 – Nov 19 | $26,000 | 14% | $60,000 | 2.3x |
| **Early-bird** | Nov 20 – Nov 26 | $14,000 | 8% | $45,000 | 3.2x |
| **BFCM core** | Nov 27 – Dec 1 | $28,000 | 15% | $140,000 | 5.0x |

I've held roughly that split but pulled a little extra into the pre-BF ramp — in a normal year October is money you'd rather not spend, but this year it's buying the bidding signal that makes November and December work at all.

## Non-negotiables before Oct 1

1. **Turn Google back on by Sept 15, not Oct 1.** Two weeks of low-budget conversion volume before the quarter starts is cheaper than relearning in November. If budget can't move, this is the one line I'd argue hardest for.
2. **Fix the Google capture failure.** It's been failing since 2026-07-31. You cannot manage a $185K quarter with a broken feed.
3. **Confirm the December shipping cut-off date and build the calendar backwards from it.** 72% of Q4 2025 revenue landed in December for a bulky foam product — the last-order date is a revenue cliff, not a footnote.
4. **Product focus:** the Original Play Castle Sofa is 81% of the last 30 days' store revenue ($1,016 of $1,254). Cover sets and personalization are attach revenue. Build the Q4 creative and Shopping feed priority around the hero SKU with attach at checkout.

## Discounting — what the code data supports (and doesn't)

Shopify discount-code coverage is COMPLETE for both quarters. Codes only capture code-applied money — **automatic and manual discounts aren't in this family**, so I can't tell you the depth of your actual BFCM sitewide offer from this, and I won't guess.

| Q4 2025 (122 codes) | Orders | Discount allocated |

| AFTERDARK | 110 | $1,650 |
| attila_test_11.25 | 5 | $1,523.61 |
| ~119 one-off personal codes | 1 each | $10–$25 each |

Three reads:

- **Your only real coded promo in either year was AFTERDARK** (110 orders, ~$15/order). Everything else in 2025 is one-off personal codes — that's customer-service discounting, 119 distinct codes deep, not a promo program. Consolidate it into 2–3 governed CS codes so it's measurable.
- **`attila_test_11.25` used a test code on 5 live orders during the Nov 2025 peak, allocating $1,523.61 — about $305 per order.** Audit and disable test codes before Oct 1.
- 2024's `2024BFCM` code was used on **11 orders** in a quarter with 4,833 orders. Whatever drove BFCM both years, it wasn't the code — so if you want to measure offer depth in Q4 2026, run the promo through a **code**, not an automatic discount.

---

Send me the promo calendar and I'll map these windows onto your real offer dates, and flag any promo that lands in the ramp window where the ROAS floor is 2.3x. **Sessions specifically: not available.** The GA4 breakdown store carries conversions and revenue at this grain, not session or user counts — every row returns clicks/impressions as 0, which is a schema limit, not a real zero. I can't give you a Q4 2024 session count from these tools without misrepresenting a field.

Worth flagging: **Direct is the single largest revenue channel at 39% of GA4 revenue**, with the highest AOV of the big three ($49.30 vs Paid Social's $22.74). With Meta at 98.7% of spend, a large share of that Direct bucket is almost certainly dark Meta traffic that lost its referrer — which is exactly why the GA-basis view understates paid social.

## 5. Bottom of funnel — store revenue and the attribution spread

Two revenue sources are present for this window, and they disagree. Both, labelled:

| Basis | Revenue | ROAS vs $393,097.48 spend |
|---|---|---|
| **Shopify (store) — the dashboard card** | **$1,069,649.43** | **2.72x** |
| GA4 (site analytics) | $945,866.32 | 2.41x |
