| Google in-platform attributed value | $694,039.06 | 134.9x (vs Google spend $5,145.70) |

**Use $1,069,649.43 and 2.72x as the headline** — that's the store basis and it's what the dashboard shows.

Why the sources diverge:

- **Shopify vs GA4: $123,783.11 gap, GA4 11.6% low.** Standard — GA4 loses orders to consent rejection, ad blockers, cross-device journeys and Safari ITP, and its revenue is click-attributed on session date while Shopify books on order date. An ~12% GA4 shortfall on a Meta-heavy account is normal, not a tracking fault.
- **Meta's $2.21M claim is not credible on a store basis.** It is **2.06x the entire store's revenue** for the quarter. Meta is crediting itself with more than double every dollar Foam OH actually took, across all channels including organic and direct. $393,097 in spend → 31.1M impressions → 496,194 clicks (1.59% CTR, $0.79 CPC) → **$1,069,649 in actual store revenue at 2.72x blended MER**.

Google was immaterial to the quarter at $5,146. On the site side, Direct out-earned everything at $370K with the highest AOV — the strongest single signal that Meta's real contribution is meaningfully larger than GA4's $195K last-click figure and meaningfully smaller than Meta's own $2.21M claim.

**Three gaps you should footnote if this goes in a document:**
1. **Meta frequency** — reach isn't captured; frequency is not derivable for this or any window.
2. **Google search terms** — read failed on our side twice (statement timeout), completeness unmeasurable. Not an empty account, an unmeasured one. I can retry month-by-month.
3. **GA4 sessions** — not carried at breakdown grain; conversions and revenue only.

Want me to go after the search terms in monthly slices, or pull Meta placement for the same quarter in 2023 to give the placement mix a baseline?

results.detail: UNGRADED — needs ground truth from captured store, coverage COMPLETE for this window
results.response:
## Q2 2025 (Apr 1 – Jun 30) — the same quarter, three different purchase counts

All figures from the **captured store**, settled through 2026-07-30. Coverage is `covered` and complete for Meta, GA4, Shopify and Google, so nothing here is a partial. This is a historical window, so there's no live snapshot to show alongside it — and note that live Google is dark right now anyway (our Google API quota is exhausted until 2026-08-01 08:03 UTC); the Google spend I reference below comes from the captured store, which is unaffected.

| Source | Purchases | Revenue on purchases | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Meta** | **70** | $14,913.50 | Ad-attributed pixel purchases, credited to ad-click/impression date |
| **GA4** | not captured as a count (see below) | **$115,634.87** | Session/tag-based purchase events, order date |
| **Shopify** | **559 orders** | **$117,840 net** ($121,067 gross) | The ledger — every order, all sources, refund-adjusted |

Shopify AOV: **$210.81**. Meta's implied AOV on its 70: **$213.05**. GA4's revenue ÷ Shopify AOV implies **~549 transactions** — that's my arithmetic, not a captured field, so treat it as an estimate.

**One honest gap:** the captured `ga_event` family for this window returns the event names (purchase, add_to_cart, begin_checkout…) but the count field came back empty, so I can't give you a hard GA4 transaction count for Q2 2025. GA4's captured `conversions` figure for the quarter is **8,151**, and that is *all conversion events combined* (add_to_cart, begin_checkout, etc.) — it is emphatically **not** 8,151 purchases. Don't let that number near a purchase comparison.

---

## Why the three numbers are different

**1. Meta's 70 is a subset by design, not a shortfall.**
Meta only counts purchases it can tie back to one of its own ads inside the attribution window (default 7-day click / 1-day view), and it stamps them on the **date of the ad interaction**, not the order date. Meta spend in Q2 was $7,780.07 against $51,166.07 on Google — 13% of the $58,946 blended spend. So the overwhelming majority of those 559 orders never touched a Meta ad and Meta correctly never claims them. 70 of 559 = **12.5% of orders**, $14,913.50 of $117,840 = **12.7% of revenue**, on 13.2% of the spend. That's proportionate, not broken.

Two Meta-specific traps in this data:
- The purchase event appears under **six alias rows** — `purchase`, `omni_purchase`, `offsite_conversion.fb_pixel_purchase`, `onsite_web_purchase`, `onsite_web_app_purchase`, `web_in_store_purchase` — all reading 70 / $14,913.50. It is **one** event surfaced six ways. Never sum them.
- Meta's value is modeled and cross-device (logged-in identity graph), and it is **never refund-adjusted**. Shopify's is.

*Meta's conversion counts here are account-level historical figures — directionally accurate but they may not reconcile perfectly with campaign-level numbers. Meta spend, clicks and impressions are exact.*

**2. GA4 is measuring the browser, on a different money basis.**
GA4 fires `purchase` from the thank-you page, on order date, attributed last-non-direct. It loses whatever consent mode, ad-blockers and ITP strip out, and it reports whatever the datalayer passes as revenue. The telling detail: GA4's $115,634.87 sits **between** Shopify net ($117,840) and Shopify total sales ($120,528.24), and is only **1.9% / $2,205 below net**. That says the tag is excluding shipping and tax like Shopify's net basis and is capturing nearly every purchase — a ~2% tracking loss is about as clean as GA4 gets. GA4 also doesn't retroactively strip refunds, so the $364 refunded in the quarter is still sitting in that figure.

**3. Shopify is the only ground truth.**
559 distinct orders, every channel, refund-adjusted as of its last re-sum. The waterfall for the quarter: gross $121,067 − $1,993 discounts = **$117,840 net**, + $2,538.24 tax + $150 shipping = $120,528.24 total sales, with $364 refunded. Shopify's net **excludes** shipping and tax — which is why it's the right thing to compare GA4 against and the wrong thing to compare against a platform's conversion value if that value is tax-inclusive.

---

## The practical rule

- **Shopify 559 / $117,840** is the denominator for anything financial — MER, blended ROAS, customer counts.
- **GA4 $115,634.87** is your channel-mix lens; it's 98.1% complete against the ledger, so its channel splits are trustworthy in *shape*.
- **Meta's 70 / $14,913.50** answers only "what did Meta's ads influence inside its own window" — a 1.92x ad-attributed ROAS on $7,780. Never add it to GA4 or Shopify; it overlaps both.

Adding all three together would triple-count roughly the same handful of real orders. The one number that would genuinely be additive — Google's $147,364.67 of ad-attributed conversion value against $51,166.07 spend — is not credible at face value either; that's 1.25x Shopify's entire quarterly revenue from one channel, which is the same over-attribution pattern we flagged in the earlier 2023/2024 Google ROAS figures. Want me to dig into which Google conversion actions are inflating that?

## Verdict: Google Ads. Unambiguously.

All figures below come from the **captured store** (settled through 2026-07-30), not the live feed — live Google is dark right now because our Google API quota is exhausted and doesn't reset until **2026-08-01 08:03 UTC**. That's an outage on our side, not a fact about the account. Coverage is `covered` for Google, Meta, Shopify and GA4 across every window here, and the result flags complete — so these are whole figures, and the zeros are real zeros.

**The setup (Q2 2025 vs Q1 2025):**

| | Q1 2025 | Q2 2025 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Store revenue (Shopify, card figure) | $69,400.30 | **$117,840.00** | **+$48,439.70 (+69.8%)** |
| GA4 revenue (second source) | $67,895.71 | $115,634.87 | +$47,739.16 (+70.3%) |
| Total ad spend | $50,963.20 | $58,946.14 | +$7,982.94 (+15.7%) |
| Google spend | $14,964.01 | **$51,166.07** | **+$36,202.06 (+242%)** |
| Meta spend | $35,999.19 | $7,780.07 | −$28,219.12 (−78%) |
| Card ROAS (store ÷ spend) | 1.36x | **2.00x** | +0.64 |

Revenue grew ~70% **while Meta spend fell by $28.2K.** Meta cannot be the growth engine — it was being defunded through the quarter. Two revenue sources are present and I'm showing both: store $117,840 (ROAS 2.00x) and GA4 $115,634.87 (ROAS 1.96x). They differ by basis — Shopify is order-date cash, GA4 is session-scoped last-click — and here they agree within 1.9%, which is unusually tight and makes the rest of this defensible.

---

## Three independent sources, three different measurement systems

### 1. Google Ads' own platform reporting (click-attributed)
| | Q1 2025 | Q2 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Spend | $14,964.01 | $51,166.07 |
| Clicks | 11,461 | 29,956 |
| Conversions | 255.8 | 682.0 |
| Ad-attributed value | $61,085.98 | $147,364.66 |
| Ad ROAS | 4.08x | 2.88x |

Google booked **+$86,278.68** of incremental attributed value on **+$36,202.06** of incremental spend — a marginal return of **2.38x**. Meta's ad-attributed value over the same shift: $116,380.80 → $14,913.50.

### 2. GA4 site analytics (independent of both ad platforms — site-side last-click)
| Source / medium | Q1 rev | Q2 rev | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| google / cpc | $19,364.20 | **$53,081.00** | **+$33,716.80** |
| (direct) / (none) | $30,415.10 | $38,899.00 | +$8,483.90 |
| google / organic | $4,880.00 | $5,401.00 | +$521.00 |
| paid social (facebook/paid + fb/paid + ig/paid) | ~$4,319.00 | $3,791.54 | −$527.46 |

**google / cpc alone is 71% of GA4-measured revenue growth** ($33,717 of $47,739). Direct is the next 18% — and part of that is untagged/repeat demand that Google's own top-of-funnel work seeds. Paid social went *down*. Breakdown coverage: COMPLETE, all 91 active days carry rows.

### 3. Shopify order records (no ad attribution at all — cash and order counts)
| Sales channel | Q1 rev / orders | Q2 rev / orders |
|---|---|---|
| web | $55,429.30 / 246 | **$108,382.00 / 508** |
| amazon | $1,872.00 / 8 | $6,768.00 / 33 |
| facebook (Shopify channel) | $1,436.00 / 7 | $863.00 / 4 |
| shop | $1,160.00 / 7 | $1,339.00 / 8 |
| tiktok | $468.00 / 2 | $199.00 / 1 |

The web storefront — where Google traffic lands — added **262 orders (+107%)** and **+$52,952.70**. Every social-adjacent channel shrank. The one non-Google bright spot is Amazon (+$4,896, 3.6x), which is real but only ~10% of the growth and isn't a paid-media effect. AOV slipped $225.32 → $213.35, so this was volume-driven, not basket-driven.

---

## Two things you should footnote before you present this

**The growth wasn't free.** Google's CPC rose $1.31 → $1.71 (+31%), CPA rose $58.51 → $75.02 (+28%), and ad ROAS compressed 4.08x → 2.88x. Google bought growth by scaling into more expensive inventory. It worked — 2.38x marginal — but the efficiency curve was bending the whole way.

**It's quarter-over-quarter growth, not recovery.** Against Q2 2024:

| | Q2 2024 | Q2 2025 |
|---|---|---|
| Store revenue | $126,988.74 | $117,840.00 (−7.2%) |
| Total spend | $46,978.54 | $58,946.14 (+25.5%) |
| Card ROAS | 2.70x | 2.00x |
| Meta / Google spend split | $34,387 / $12,591 | $7,780 / $51,166 |

So the honest framing on your Andromeda thesis: the channel mix inverted completely year-over-year, and Google's scale-up recovered **93% of last year's revenue on 26% more spend**. Google drove the Q2 2025 growth — but what it was doing was backfilling a Meta hole, at roughly 0.74x the blended efficiency the account had a year earlier.

Q1/Q2 2025 are historical windows anyway, so there's no live counterpart to show alongside them.

---

# The headline: a channel swap, not a growth push

| | Q1 2025 | Q2 2025 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Total ad spend** | $50,963.20 | $58,946.14 | **+15.7%** |
| — Google | $14,964.01 (29%) | $51,166.07 (**87%**) | **+242%** |
| — Meta | $35,999.19 (71%) | $7,780.07 (**13%**) | **−78%** |
| **Shopify revenue (card)** | $69,400.30 | $117,840.00 | **+69.8%** |
| **Blended ROAS (store basis)** | **1.36x** | **2.00x** | +47% |
| GA4 revenue | $67,895.71 | $115,634.87 | +70.3% |
| GA-basis ROAS | 1.33x | 1.96x | +47% |
| Shopify orders | 479 | 844 | +76% |
| AOV | $144.89 | $139.62 | −3.6% |
| Impressions | 8.45M | 6.60M | −22% |
| Clicks | 99,796 | 43,693 | −56% |
| CTR / CPC | 1.18% / $0.51 | 0.66% / $1.35 | — |

Store and GA revenue sit within 2% of each other in both quarters (basis differs — Shopify is order-level, GA4 is session-attributed on purchase date), so the story is the same on either measurement. Use the store figures as the card numbers.

**You spent 16% more and made 70% more.** Almost all of the delta is one decision.

---

## What actually caused it: the May pivot

| 2025 | Meta spend | Google spend | Store revenue | Blended ROAS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan | $20,743.58 | $2,404.64 | $22,988 | 0.99x |
| Feb | $5,781.57 | $3,545.55 | $18,162 | 1.95x |
| Mar | $9,474.04 | $9,013.82 | $28,250 | 1.53x |
| Apr | $5,310.64 | $6,433.73 | $15,711 | **1.34x** ← trough |
| **May** | **$1,306.83** | **$21,963.89** | **$47,164** | **2.03x** |
| Jun | $1,162.60 | $22,768.45 | $54,965 | **2.30x** |

The quarter-over-quarter numbers hide the fact that this wasn't a Q1→Q2 drift — it's a step change dated to **May 1**. April was the worst month of the half (revenue $15,711, ROAS 1.34x). In May Google went from $6.4K to $22.0K/month and Meta effectively went dark at ~$1.2K/month. Revenue tripled off the April trough and held in June.

**Where the incremental Google money landed:** GA4 channel revenue shows Cross-network (Performance Max) going **$19,231 → $54,796, +185%** — that single channel accounts for $35.6K of the $47.7K GA revenue gain. Direct added $8.5K ($30,415 → $38,899), which is the usual PMax halo/attribution spillover. Organic Search added $1.9K. Paid Social *fell* slightly ($4,319 → $3,951) despite $7.8K still going into Meta.

---

## The efficiency picture underneath

**Google — scaled into thinner air, but still accretive:**
- Ad-attributed conversion value $61,086 → $147,365 (+141%)
- Ad ROAS 4.08x → 2.88x
- CPC $1.31 → $1.71 (+31%), CPA $58.51 → $75.02 (+28%)

Classic scaling curve: 3.4x the budget bought 2.4x the value. Marginal efficiency degraded ~30%, but the channel stayed well above the blended line, which is why the account-level ROAS rose even as Google's own ROAS fell.

**Meta — degraded faster than it shrank:**
- Spend −78%, but conversions 731 → 69 (**−91%**)
- CTR 1.25% → 0.51%, CPA $49.25 → $112.75, ad ROAS 3.09x → 1.89x

*(Meta conversion counts and CPA here are account-level historical figures — directionally accurate but they may not reconcile perfectly with campaign-level numbers. Meta spend, clicks and impressions are exact.)*

---

## On the Andromeda read — this window complicates it

Q2 does show Meta quality deteriorating: CTR halved and CPA more than doubled. But two things cut against reading this quarter as Andromeda damage:

1. **The degradation is confounded with the shutdown.** At $1,307 (May) and $1,163 (June), Meta is running below any meaningful learning threshold — a couple of hundred dollars a week across the account. Delivery quality collapsing at that budget is expected regardless of what changed in the auction. You cannot separate "the audiences broke" from "we starved the channel" inside Q2.
2. **The business got better, not worse.** Blended ROAS went 1.36x → 2.00x and orders +76% in exactly the quarter Meta was withdrawn. Whatever happened to Meta, the reallocation to Google PMax more than paid for it.

The place to actually test the Andromeda thesis is the *pre-pullback* window — Nov '24 through April '25, while Meta was still funded at $5K–$20K/month — not Q2, where the signal is buried under a 78% budget cut.

---

## The open question

Google's marginal CPA rose 28% getting to $51K/quarter, and June was already flattening ($22.8K spend for $55.0K store revenue vs May's $22.0K → $47.2K — better, but the curve is bending). Worth knowing whether the May pivot was a deliberate reallocation or a Meta pause that Google absorbed by default, because those imply different Q3 plans. I can pull Google's search terms, PMax asset-group detail, or impression share for May–June to show how much headroom was left — say the word.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oct 2025 | $10,187 | $26,132 | 2.57x | 3.7% |

**The single fact that dominates this forecast: the account has been at zero paid spend for three months.** Revenue is now ~$1.5–2.2K/month of pure organic/direct. Q4 2026 is not a demand question, it's a budget-decision question.

---

## Q4 2026 forecast (Oct 1 – Dec 31)

Organic-only baseline from the three zero-spend months: **~$2,200/mo**, with a Q4 uplift applied (I used 1.5x / 2.5x / 4.5x for Oct/Nov/Dec — softer than 2025's 3.7/24/72 split, because that curve was promo- and budget-driven, not organic).

| Scenario | Q4 Google spend | Store rev — point | 80% range | Implied MER |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Stays dark** (status quo) | $0 | **$18K** | $10K – $30K | n/a |
| **B. Modest restart** ($5K/$9K/$16K) | $30K | **$78K** | $58K – $105K | 2.6x |
| **C. Match last Q4** (Oct $10K/Nov $38K/Dec $135K) | $183K | **$475K** | $360K – $640K | 2.6x |

GA4-basis equivalents: multiply by **0.89**.

**Why B and C assume 2.6x MER, not last year's 3.84x:**
1. Cold start. The March 2026 restart spent $15,138 and returned 1.66x — that's your only recent evidence of what re-lighting this account looks like after a dark period, and it's less than half of Q4 2025's efficiency.
2. Auction inflation. Google CPC went $1.22 (Sep '25) → $3.01 (Dec '25). Expect that again.
3. Underlying demand decay. GA4 Q1 2026 ($56,204) was down ~17% on Q1 2025 (~$67.9K) on comparable spend. That's the structural drift, separate from the budget cut.
4. Five months of dark means lost conversion signal, cold audience/remarketing pools, and a Performance Max/Shopping learning reset.

**Rest of Q3 2026 (Aug–Sep), if nothing changes:** ~$4K–6K store revenue. Q3 2026 will land near **$6K–8K** versus Q3 2025's $172,350 — a 96% decline, entirely budget-driven.

---

## Uncertainty — stated plainly

**Confidence: low-to-moderate, and asymmetric.**

- **The spend decision is not a forecast input I can estimate — it's exogenous.** The spread between A and C is 26x. Everything else is noise by comparison. Until you tell me the Q4 budget, this is three scenarios, not a forecast.
- **The organic baseline rests on n=3 months** (May $3,752, Jun $1,054, Jul $1,826), and they're non-monotonic. At 7 orders/month, one Castle Sofa order moves the monthly number ±15%. That's why Scenario A's range is ±60% around its point.
- **The Q4 organic seasonality multiplier is my weakest assumption.** I have no clean zero-spend Q4 in the history to calibrate against — every prior Q4 had heavy paid support, so I cannot separate organic seasonality from paid seasonality. I inferred it conservatively.
- **Concentration risk isn't in the model.** The Original Play Castle Sofa is $1,016 of July's $1,254 GA-basis revenue (81%). A stockout, price change or listing issue on one SKU breaks every scenario.
- **Meta is modelled at zero.** If Meta relights, all three scenarios are void — and note Q4 2024 was $388K of Meta spend at 2.72x blended, so that lever is materially larger than anything Google-side.
- **Lead time matters and is running out.** Q4 2025 earned 4.50x in November partly because October's $10K was already feeding the algorithm. A December-only restart will underperform Scenario B's efficiency, not match it.

**What would tighten this most, in order:** (1) the Q4 budget number and start date, (2) the targets file, (3) 3–4 weeks of live spend post-restart to re-measure marginal MER — after which I can replace the 2.6x assumption with a measured one.

## Q2 2026 vs Q2 2021 — Influential Drones

Two notes on sourcing before the numbers. Live Google data can't be fetched right now — our Google API quota is exhausted platform-wide and doesn't reset until 2026-08-01 08:03 UTC — so **every Google figure below comes from the captured store**, which is what the dashboard cards use and is unaffected by the outage. And for Q2 2021, GA4 and Meta both **predate our capture floors** (GA from 2023-06-22, Meta from 2024-09-17), so there is no measured data for them in that quarter — that's a coverage gap, not zero activity. Shopify (floor 2019-04-13) and Google (floor 2018-08-11) cover both quarters cleanly.

| | Q2 2021 | Q2 2026 | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Store revenue (canonical)** | $149,135.49 | $403,353.05 | **+170%** |
| Google spend | $461.41 | $4,107.85 | +790% |
| Blended ROAS (store rev ÷ spend) | 323.2x | 98.2x | −70% |
| Impressions | 153,383 | 17,016 | −89% |
| Clicks | 995 | 870 | −13% |
| CTR | 0.65% | 5.11% | +686% |
| CPC | $0.46 | $4.72 | +926% |
| Google conversions | 51 | 126 | +147% |
| Google CPA | $9.05 | $32.60 | +260% |
| Units sold (store) | 218 | 184 | −16% |
| **Revenue per unit** | $684.11 | $2,192.67 | **+220%** |

### The real story: same volume, triple the deal size

Revenue nearly tripled on **fewer units** (184 vs 218). Average value per line item went from $684 to $2,193. This is no longer the same business — it's shifted from accessory/small-hardware e-commerce to high-ticket institutional deals.

Media follows the same shift. The 2021 account was a cheap, broad-reach setup (153K impressions at $0.46/click, 0.65% CTR). The 2026 account is a tight, intent-heavy one: 89% fewer impressions, near-identical click volume, and a 5.11% CTR. The higher CPC and CPA are the *price* of that intent, and at 98x blended ROAS the trade is clearly working — a 70% ROAS decline off a 323x base while revenue grew $254K is a healthy dilution, not a problem.

**Two revenue sources in Q2 2026 and they disagree:** Shopify store = **$403,353.05** (98.2x on Google spend); GA4 = **$36,559.63** (8.9x). GA4 only captures on-site checkout with a session it can attribute, so quote-based/offline-closed deals never appear there. Shopify is the correct headline. GA4 has no counterpart in Q2 2021, so that split can't be trended.

### What to focus on

Q2 2026 product-type revenue breaks down as:

| Product type | Revenue | Share |
|---|---|---|
| **UNKNOWN (untyped)** | $353,983.11 | 87.7% |
| Drones | $22,152.83 | 5.5% |
| Event | $12,570.00 | 3.1% |
| Training | $8,113.00 | 2.0% |
| Battery | $4,220.70 | 1.0% |
| Countermeasures | $1,190.00 | 0.3% |
| Propeller / LED / Accessories / Charger / Safety | $1,123.41 | 0.3% |

**Focus on the high-ticket institutional line — NIST test-method apparatus and the agency training/event programs.** That's where the $2,193-per-unit average lives, and it matches what's happening right now: the two largest orders in the last 30 days are custom deals at $17,490 and $14,740, with the NIST Aerial Test Method Level 1-3 Portable Apparatus Set at $3,897 behind them. In GA4, `/products/suas-level-1-3-test-method-nist-portable-set` converts at **1.61%** — the only landing page above 1%, and ~10x the site average of 0.16% on the homepage. That page is the proven money route and deserves the paid budget.

The catalog accessories (propellers, LEDs, chargers, speakers — $1,123 combined for the quarter) are not worth media spend at a $4.72 CPC. They're attach-rate items, not acquisition items.

**One fix worth doing this week:** 87.7% of Q2 revenue sits in `UNKNOWN` product type. Those are almost certainly the custom deal line items, and until they're typed you can't segment, feed them to Shopping, or build lookalikes off them. Tagging that $354K into real categories is the single highest-leverage data task on this account — coverage on the breakdown was complete across all 39 active days, so this is a taxonomy gap, not a capture gap.

### What's actually driving it

Growth is **entirely volume-led**. Orders climbed 37.6% while AOV fell 12.9% — so the store sold a lot more, at meaningfully smaller basket sizes. Had 2025 held 2024's $103.78 AOV, 651 orders would have produced roughly **$67.6k** instead of $58.8k, so the AOV compression cost about **$8.7k** of potential revenue.

That pattern is consistent with what we've seen more recently — discount-driven and entry-price SKUs (Discovery Kit-type products) pulling in order count while diluting basket value.
